entries.7a94c4d58a1ee886f41668869a7cc913df3396b5: <div sID="gen31125" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="7" osisID="1Cor.7" sID="1Cor.7"/> <div eID="gen31125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31126" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31127" type="x-p"/> In this chapter the apostle answers some cases proposed to him by the Corinthians about marriage. He, I. Shows them that marriage was appointed as a remedy against fornication, and therefore that persons had better marry than burn, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.1-1Cor.7.9">ver. 1-9</reference>. II. He gives direction to those who are married to continue together, though they might have an unbelieving relative, unless the unbeliever would part, in which case a Christian would not be in bondage, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.10-1Cor.7.16">ver. 10-16</reference>. III. He shows them that becoming Christians does not change their external state; and therefore advises every one to continue, in the general, in that state in which he was called, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.17-1Cor.7.24">ver. 17-24</reference>. IV. He advises them, by reason of the present distress, to keep themselves unmarried; hints the shortness of time, and how they should improve it, so as to grow dead and indifferent to the comforts of the world; and shows them how worldly cares hinder their devotions, and distract them in the service of God, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.25-1Cor.7.35">ver. 25-35</reference>. V. He directs them in the disposal of their virgins, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.36-1Cor.7.38">ver. 36-38</reference>. VI. And closes the chapter with advice to widows how to dispose of themselves in that state, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.39-1Cor.7.40">ver. 39, 40</reference>.
entries.4463044f61568898b6584ba4b9735ac26f83c95c: <div eID="gen31127" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31126" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Against Fornication. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31128" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now concerning the things whereof ye wrote unto me: <hi type="italic">It is</hi> good for a man not to touch a woman. <hi type="super">2</hi> Nevertheless, <hi type="italic">to avoid</hi> fornication, let every man have his own wife, and let every woman have her own husband. <hi type="super">3</hi> Let the husband render unto the wife due benevolence: and likewise also the wife unto the husband. <hi type="super">4</hi> The wife hath not power of her own body, but the husband: and likewise also the husband hath not power of his own body, but the wife. <hi type="super">5</hi> Defraud ye not one the other, except <hi type="italic">it be</hi> with consent for a time, that ye may give yourselves to fasting and prayer; and come together again, that Satan tempt you not for your incontinency. <hi type="super">6</hi> But I speak this by permission, <hi type="italic">and</hi> not of commandment. <hi type="super">7</hi> For I would that all men were even as I myself. But every man hath his proper gift of God, one after this manner, and another after that. <hi type="super">8</hi> I say therefore to the unmarried and widows, It is good for them if they abide even as I. <hi type="super">9</hi> But if they cannot contain, let them marry: for it is better to marry than to burn. <div eID="gen31128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31129" type="x-p"/> The apostle comes now, as a faithful and skilful casuist, to answer some cases of conscience which the Corinthians had proposed to him. Those were <hi type="italic">things whereof they wrote to him,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.1">v. 1</reference>. As the lips of ministers should <hi type="italic">keep knowledge,</hi> so the people should <hi type="italic">ask the law at their mouths.</hi> The apostle was as ready to resolve as they were to propose their doubts. In the former chapter, he warns them to avoid fornication; here he gives some directions about marriage, the remedy God had appointed for it. He tells them in general, <div eID="gen31129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31130" type="x-p"/> I. That it was good, in that juncture of time at least, to abstain from marriage altogether: <hi type="italic">It is good for a man not to touch a woman</hi> (not to take her to wife), by good here not understanding what is so conformable to the mind and will of God as if to do otherwise were sin, an extreme into which many of the ancients have run in favour of celibacy and virginity. Should the apostle be understood in this sense, he would contradict much of the rest of his discourse. But it is good, that is, either abstracting from circumstances there are many things in which the state of celibacy has the advantage above the marriage state; or else <hi type="italic">at this juncture,</hi> by reason of the distress of the Christian church, it would be a convenience for Christians to keep themselves single, provided they have the gift of continency, and at the same time can keep themselves chaste. The expression also may carry in it an intimation that Christians must avoid all occasions of this sin, and flee all fleshly lusts, and incentives to them; must neither look on nor touch a woman, so as to provoke lustful inclinations. Yet, <div eID="gen31130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31131" type="x-p"/> II. He informs them that marriage, and the comforts and satisfactions of that state, are by divine wisdom prescribed for preventing fornication (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.2">v. 2</reference>), <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Porneias</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">Fornications,</hi> all sorts of lawless lust. To avoid these, <hi type="italic">Let every man,</hi> says he, <hi type="italic">have his own wife, and every woman her own husband;</hi> that is, marry, and confine themselves to their own mates. And, when they are married, let each render the other <hi type="italic">due benevolence</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.3">v. 3</reference>), consider the disposition and exigency of each other, and render conjugal duty, which is owing to each other. For, as the apostle argues (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.4">v. 4</reference>), in the married state neither person has power over his own body, but has delivered it into the power of the other, the wife hers into the power of the husband, the husband his into the power of the wife. Note, Polygamy, or the marriage of more persons than one, as well as adultery, must be a breach of marriage-covenants, and a violation of the partner's rights. And therefore they should not defraud one another of the use of their bodies, nor any other of the comforts of the conjugal state, appointed of God for keeping <hi type="italic">the vessel in sanctification and honour,</hi> and preventing the lusts of uncleanness, except it be <hi type="italic">with mutual consent</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.5">v. 5</reference>) and <hi type="italic">for a time</hi> only, while they employ themselves in some extraordinary duties of religion, <hi type="italic">or give themselves to fasting and prayer.</hi> Note, Seasons of deep humiliation require abstinence from lawful pleasures. But this separation between husband and wife must not be for a continuance, lest they expose themselves to Satan's temptations, by reason of their incontinence, or inability to contain. Note, Persons expose themselves to great danger by attempting to perform what is above their strength, and at the same time not bound upon them by any law of God. If they abstain from lawful enjoyments, they may be ensnared into unlawful ones. The remedies God hath provided against sinful inclinations are certainly best. <div eID="gen31131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31132" type="x-p"/> III. The apostle limits what he had said about <hi type="italic">every man's having his own wife,</hi> &c. (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">I speak this by permission, not of command.</hi> He did not lay it as an injunction upon every man to marry without exception. Any man might marry. No law of God prohibited the thing. But, on the other hand, not law bound a man to marry so that he sinned if he did not; I mean, unless his circumstances required it for preventing the lust of uncleanness. It was a thing in which men, by the laws of God, were in a great measure left at liberty. And therefore Paul did not bind every man to marry, though every man had an allowance. No, he <hi type="italic">could wish all men were as himself</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.7">v. 7</reference>), that is, single, and capable of living continently in that state. There were several conveniences in it, which at that season, if not at others, made it more eligible in itself. Note, It is a mark of true goodness to wish all men as happy as ourselves. But it did not answer the intentions of divine Providence as well for all men to have as much command of this appetite as Paul had. It was a gift vouchsafed to such persons as Infinite Wisdom thought proper: <hi type="italic">Every one hath his proper gift of God, one after this manner and another after that.</hi> Natural constitutions vary; and, where there may not be much difference in the constitution, different degrees of grace are vouchsafed, which may give some a greater victory over natural inclination than others. Note, The gifts of God, both in nature and grace, are variously distributed. Some have them after this manner and some after that. Paul could wish all men were as himself, but <hi type="italic">all men cannot receive such a saying, save those to whom it is given,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.19.11">Matt. xix. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen31132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31133" type="x-p"/> IV. He sums up his sense on this head (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.9-1Cor.7.10">v. 9, 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">I say therefore to the unmarried and widows,</hi> to those in a state of virginity or widowhood, <hi type="italic">It is good for them if they abide even as I.</hi> There are many conveniences, and especially at this juncture, in a single state, to render it preferable to a married one. It is convenient therefore <hi type="italic">that the unmarried abide as I,</hi> which plainly implies that Paul was at that time unmarried. <hi type="italic">But, if they cannot contain, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn.</hi> This is God's remedy for lust. The fire may be quenched by the means he has appointed. And marriage, with all its inconveniences, is much better than to burn with impure and lustful desires. <hi type="italic">Marriage is honourable in all;</hi> but it is a duty in those who cannot contain nor conquer those inclinations.
entries.32308b2c53a9ddb1ab8f8179e6da660f3615b7c5: <div eID="gen31133" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Inviolability of the Marriage Bond. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31134" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> And unto the married I command, <hi type="italic">yet</hi> not I, but the Lord, Let not the wife depart from <hi type="italic">her</hi> husband: <hi type="super">11</hi> But and if she depart, let her remain unmarried, or be reconciled to <hi type="italic">her</hi> husband: and let not the husband put away <hi type="italic">his</hi> wife. <hi type="super">12</hi> But to the rest speak I, not the Lord: If any brother hath a wife that believeth not, and she be pleased to dwell with him, let him not put her away. <hi type="super">13</hi> And the woman which hath a husband that believeth not, and if he be pleased to dwell with her, let her not leave him. <hi type="super">14</hi> For the unbelieving husband is sanctified by the wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified by the husband: else were your children unclean; but now are they holy. <hi type="super">15</hi> But if the unbelieving depart, let him depart. A brother or a sister is not under bondage in such <hi type="italic">cases:</hi> but God hath called us to peace. <hi type="super">16</hi> For what knowest thou, O wife, whether thou shalt save <hi type="italic">thy</hi> husband? or how knowest thou, O man, whether thou shalt save <hi type="italic">thy</hi> wife? <div eID="gen31134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31135" type="x-p"/> In this paragraph the apostle gives them direction in a case which must be very frequent in that age of the world, especially among the Jewish converts; I mean whether they were to live with heathen relatives in a married state. Moses's law permitted divorce; and there was a famous instance in the Jewish state, when the people were obliged to put away their idolatrous wives, <reference osisRef="Ezra.10.3">Ezra x. 3</reference>. This might move a scruple in many minds, whether converts to Christianity were not bound to put away or desert their mates, continuing infidels. Concerning this matter the apostle here gives direction. And, <div eID="gen31135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31136" type="x-p"/> I. In general, he tells them that marriage, by Christ's command, is for life; and therefore those who are married must not think of separation. The wife <hi type="italic">must not depart from the husband</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.10">v. 10</reference>), nor the <hi type="italic">husband put away his wife,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.11">v. 11</reference>. This <hi type="italic">I command,</hi> says the apostle; <hi type="italic">yet not I, but the Lord.</hi> Not that he commanded any thing of his own head, or upon his own authority. Whatever he commanded was the Lord's command, dictated by his Spirit and enjoined by his authority. But his meaning is that the Lord himself, with his own mouth, had forbidden such separations, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.32">Matt. v. 32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.19.9">xix. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.10.11">Mark x. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.16.18">Luke xvi. 18</reference>. Note, Man and wife cannot separate at pleasure, nor dissolve, when they will, their matrimonial bonds and relation. They must not separate for any other cause than what Christ allows. And therefore the apostle advises that if any woman had been separated, either by a voluntary act of her own or by an act of her husband, she should continue unmarried, and seek reconciliation with her husband, that they might cohabit again. Note, Husbands and wives should not quarrel at all, or should be quickly reconciled. They are bound to each other for life. The divine law allows of no separation. They cannot throw off the burden, and therefore should set their shoulders to it, and endeavour to make it as light to each other as they can. <div eID="gen31136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31137" type="x-p"/> II. He brings the general advice home to the case of such as had an unbelieving mate (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">But to the rest speak I, not the Lord;</hi> that is, the Lord had not so expressly spoken to this case as to the former divorce. It does not mean that the apostle spoke without authority from the Lord, or decided this case by his own wisdom, without the inspiration of the Holy Ghost. He closes this subject with a declaration to the contrary (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.40">v. 40</reference>), I think <hi type="italic">also that I have the Spirit of God.</hi> But, having thus prefaced his advice, we may attend, <div eID="gen31137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31138" type="x-p"/> 1. To the advice itself, which is that if an unbelieving husband or wife were pleased to dwell with a Christian relative, the other should not separate. The husband should not put away an unbelieving wife, nor the wife leave an unbelieving husband, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.12-1Cor.7.13">v. 12, 13</reference>. The Christian calling did not dissolve the marriage covenant, but bind it the faster, by bringing it back to the original institution, limiting it to two persons, and binding them together for life. The believer is not by faith in Christ loosed from matrimonial bonds to an unbeliever, but is at once bound and made apt to be a better relative. But, though a believing wife or husband should not separate from an unbelieving mate, yet if the unbelieving relative desert the believer, and no means can reconcile to a cohabitation, in such <hi type="italic">a case a brother or sister is not in bondage</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.15">v. 15</reference>), not tied up to the unreasonable humour, and bound servilely to follow or cleave to the malicious deserter, or not bound to live unmarried after all proper means for reconciliation have been tried, at least of the deserter contract another marriage or be guilty of adultery, which was a very easy supposition, because a very common instance among the heathen inhabitants of Corinth. In such a case the deserted person must be free to marry again, and it is granted on all hands. And some think that such a malicious desertion is as much a dissolution of the marriage-covenant as death itself. For how is it possible that <hi type="italic">the two shall be one flesh</hi> when the one is maliciously bent to part from or put away the other? Indeed, the deserter seems still bound by the matrimonial contract; and therefore the apostle says (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.11">v. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">If the woman depart from her husband</hi> upon the account of his infidelity, <hi type="italic">let her remain unmarried.</hi> But the deserted party seems to be left more at liberty (I mean supposing all the proper means have been used to reclaim the deserter, and other circumstances make it necessary) to marry another person. It does not seem reasonable that they should be still bound, when it is rendered impossible to perform conjugal duties or enjoy conjugal comforts, through the mere fault of their mate: in such a case marriage would be a state of servitude indeed. But, whatever liberty be indulged Christians in such a case as this, they are not allowed, for the mere infidelity of a husband or wife, to separate; but, if the unbeliever be willing, they should continue in the relation, and cohabit as those who are thus related. This is the apostle's general direction. <div eID="gen31138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31139" type="x-p"/> 2. We have here the reasons of this advice. (1.) Because the relation or state is sanctified by the holiness of either party: <hi type="italic">For the unbelieving husband is sanctified by the wife, and the unbelieving wife by the husband</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.14">v. 14</reference>), or <hi type="italic">hath been sanctified.</hi> The relation itself, and the conjugal use of each other, are sanctified to the believer. <hi type="italic">To the pure all things are pure,</hi> <reference osisRef="Titus.1.15">Tit. i. 15</reference>. Marriage is a divine institution; it is a compact for life, by God's appointment. Had converse and congress with unbelievers in that relation defiled the believer, or rendered him or her offensive to God, the ends of marriage would have been defeated, and the comforts of it in a manner destroyed, in the circumstances in which Christians then were. But the apostle tells them that, though they were yoked with unbelievers, yet, if they themselves were holy, marriage was to them a holy state, and marriage comforts, even with an unbelieving relative, were sanctified enjoyments. It was no more displeasing to God for them to continue to live as they did before, with their unbelieving or heathen relation, than if they had become converts together. If one of the relatives had become holy, nothing of the duties or lawful comforts of the married state could defile them, and render them displeasing to God, though the other were a heathen. He is sanctified for the wife's sake. She is sanctified for the husband's sake. Both are one flesh. He is to be reputed clean who is one flesh with her that is holy, and <hi type="italic">vice vers&#226;: Else were your children unclean, but now are they holy</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.14">v. 14</reference>), that is, they would be heathen, out of the pale of the church and covenant of God. They would not be of the holy seed (as the Jews are called, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.13">Isa. vi. 13</reference>), but common and unclean, in the same sense as heathens in general were styled in the apostle's vision, <reference osisRef="Acts.10.28">Acts x. 28</reference>. This way of speaking is according to the dialect of the Jews, among whom a child begotten by parents yet heathens, was said to be begotten <hi type="italic">out of holiness;</hi> and a child begotten by parents made proselytes was said to be begotten <hi type="italic">intra sanctitatem—within the holy enclosure.</hi> Thus Christians are called commonly <hi type="italic">saints;</hi> such they are by profession, separated to be a peculiar people of God, and as such distinguished from the world; and therefore the children born to Christians, though married to unbelievers, are not to be reckoned as part of the world, but of the church, a holy, not a common and unclean seed. "Continue therefore to live even with unbelieving relatives; for, if you are holy, the relation is so, the state is so, you may make a holy use even of an unbelieving relative, in conjugal duties, and your seed will be holy too." What a comfort is this, where both relatives are believers! (2.) Another reason is that <hi type="italic">God hath called Christians to peace,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.15">v. 15</reference>. The Christian religion obliges us to act peaceably in all relations, natural and civil. We are bound, <hi type="italic">as much as in us lies, to live peaceably with all men</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.12.18">Rom. xii. 18</reference>), and therefore surely to promote the peace and comfort of our nearest relatives, those with whom we are one flesh, nay, though they should be infidels. Note, It should be the labour and study of those who are married to make each other as easy and happy as possible. (3.) A third reason is that it is possible for the believing relative to be an instrument of the other's salvation (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">What knowest thou, O wife, whether thou shalt save thy husband?</hi> Note, It is the plain duty of those in so near a relation to seek the salvation of those to whom they are related. "Do not separate. There is other duty now called for. The conjugal relation calls for the most close and endeared affection; it is a contract for life. And should a Christian desert a mate, when an opportunity offers to give the most glorious proof of love? Stay, and labour heartily for the conversion of thy relative. Endeavour to save a soul. Who knows but this may be the event? It is not impossible. And, though there be no great probability, saving a soul is so good and glorious a service that the bare possibility should put one on exerting one's self." Note, Mere possibility of success should be a sufficient motive with us to use our diligent endeavours for saving the souls of our relations. "<hi type="italic">What know I but I may save his soul?</hi> should move me to attempt it."
entries.d0a23b08129bba6a1b756891482ad7f4bc785d7c: <div eID="gen31139" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christian Contentment. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31140" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> But as God hath distributed to every man, as the Lord hath called every one, so let him walk. And so ordain I in all churches. <hi type="super">18</hi> Is any man called being circumcised? let him not become uncircumcised. Is any called in uncircumcision? let him not be circumcised. <hi type="super">19</hi> Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the keeping of the commandments of God. <hi type="super">20</hi> Let every man abide in the same calling wherein he was called. <hi type="super">21</hi> Art thou called <hi type="italic">being</hi> a servant? care not for it: but if thou mayest be made free, use <hi type="italic">it</hi> rather. 22 For he that is called in the Lord, <hi type="italic">being</hi> a servant, is the Lord's freeman: likewise also he that is called, <hi type="italic">being</hi> free, is Christ's servant. <hi type="super">23</hi> Ye are bought with a price; be not ye the servants of men. <hi type="super">24</hi> Brethren, let every man, wherein he is called, therein abide with God. <div eID="gen31140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31141" type="x-p"/> Here the apostle takes occasion to advise them to continue in the state and condition in which Christianity found them, and in which they became converts to it. And here, <div eID="gen31141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31142" type="x-p"/> I. He lays down this rule in general—<hi type="italic">as God hath distributed to every one.</hi> Note, Our states and circumstances in this world are distributions of divine Providence. <hi type="italic">This fixes the bounds of men's habitations,</hi> and orders their steps. God setteth up and pulleth down. And again, <hi type="italic">As the Lord hath called every one, so let him walk.</hi> Whatever his circumstances or condition was when he was converted to Christianity, let him abide therein, and suit his conversation to it. The rules of Christianity reach every condition. And in every state a man may live so as to be a credit to it. Note, It is the duty of every Christian to suit his behaviour to his condition and the rules of religion, to be content with his lot, and conduct himself in his rank and place as becomes a Christian. The apostle adds that this was a general rule, to be observed at all times and in all places; <hi type="italic">So ordain I in all churches.</hi> <div eID="gen31142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31143" type="x-p"/> II. He specifies particular cases; as, 1. That of circumcision. <hi type="italic">Is any man called being circumcised? Let him not be uncircumcised. Is any man called being uncircumcised? Let him not be circumcised.</hi> It matters not whether a man be a Jew or Gentile, within the covenant of peculiarity made with Abraham or without it. He who is converted, being a Jew, has no need to give himself uneasiness upon that head, and wish himself uncircumcised. Nor, is he who is converted from Gentilism under an obligation to be circumcised: nor should he be concerned because he wants that mark of distinction which did heretofore belong to the people of God. For, as the apostle goes on, <hi type="italic">circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but keeping the commandments of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.19">v. 19</reference>. In point of acceptance with God, it is neither here nor there whether men be circumcised or not. Note, It is practical religion, sincere obedience to the commands of God, on which the gospel lays stress. External observances without internal piety are as nothing. Therefore let every man abide <hi type="italic">in the calling</hi> (the state) <hi type="italic">wherein he was called,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.20">v. 20</reference>. 2. That of servitude and freedom. It was common in that age of the world for many to be in a state of slavery, bought and sold for money, and so the property of those who purchased them. "Now," says the apostle, "<hi type="italic">art thou called being a servant? Care not for it.</hi> Be not over-solicitous about it. It is not inconsistent with thy duty, profession, or hopes, as a Christian. <hi type="italic">Yet, if thou mayest be made free, use it rather,</hi>" <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.21">v. 21</reference>. There are many conveniences in a state of freedom above that of servitude: a man has more power over himself, and more command of his time, and is not under the control of another lord; and therefore liberty is the more eligible state. But men's outward condition does neither hinder nor promote their acceptance with God. For he that is called <hi type="italic">being a servant is the Lord's freed-man</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">apeleutheros,</hi></hi> <hi type="italic">as he that is called being free is the Lord's servant.</hi> Though he be not discharged from his master's service, he is freed from the dominion and vassalage of sin. Though he be not enslaved to Christ, yet he is bound to yield himself up wholly to his pleasure and service; and yet that service is perfect freedom. Note, Our comfort and happiness depend on what we are to Christ, not what we are in the world. The goodness of our outward condition does not discharge us from the duties of Christianity, nor the badness of it debar us from Christian privileges. He who is a slave may yet be a Christian freeman; he who is a freeman may yet be Christ's servant. He is bought with a price, and should not therefore be the servant of man. Not that he must quit the service of his master, or not take all proper measures to please him (this were to contradict the whole scope of the apostle's discourse); but he must not be so the servant of men but that Christ's will must be obeyed, and regarded, more than his master's. He has paid a much dearer price for him, and has a much fuller property in him. He is to be served and obeyed without limitation or reserve. Note, The servants of Christ should be at the absolute command of no other master besides himself, should serve no man, any further than is consistent with their duty to him. <hi type="italic">No man can serve two masters.</hi> Though some understand this passage of persons being bought out of slavery by the bounty and charity of fellow-Christians; and read the passage thus, <hi type="italic">Have you been redeemed out of slavery with a price? Do not again become enslaved;</hi> just as before he had advised that, if in slavery they had any prospect of being made free, they should choose it rather. This meaning the words will bear, but the other seems the more natural. See <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.20">ch. vi. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen31143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31144" type="x-p"/> III. He sums up his advice: <hi type="italic">Let every man wherein he is called abide therein with God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.24">v. 24</reference>. This is to be understood of the state wherein a man is converted to Christianity. No man should make his faith or religion an argument to break through any natural or civil obligations. He should quietly and comfortably abide in the condition in which he is; and this he may well do, when he may abide therein with God. Note, The special presence and favour of God are not limited to any outward condition or performance. He may enjoy it who is circumcised; and so may he who is uncircumcised. He who is bound may have it as well as he who is free. In this respect <hi type="italic">there is neither Greek nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, barbarian nor Scythian, bond nor free,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.3.11">Col. iii. 11</reference>. The favour of God is not bound.
entries.f73a39530cd026a031d42f6dee253e4e4c1a3a21: <div eID="gen31144" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Prudential Directions to Virgins. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31145" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">25</hi> Now concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord: yet I give my judgment, as one that hath obtained mercy of the Lord to be faithful. <hi type="super">26</hi> I suppose therefore that this is good for the present distress, <hi type="italic">I say,</hi> that <hi type="italic">it is</hi> good for a man so to be. <hi type="super">27</hi> Art thou bound unto a wife? seek not to be loosed. Art thou loosed from a wife? seek not a wife. <hi type="super">28</hi> But and if thou marry, thou hast not sinned; and if a virgin marry, she hath not sinned. Nevertheless such shall have trouble in the flesh: but I spare you. <hi type="super">29</hi> But this I say, brethren, the time <hi type="italic">is</hi> short: it remaineth, that both they that have wives be as though they had none; <hi type="super">30</hi> And they that weep, as though they wept not; and they that rejoice, as though they rejoiced not; and they that buy, as though they possessed not; <hi type="super">31</hi> And they that use this world, as not abusing <hi type="italic">it:</hi> for the fashion of this world passeth away. 32 But I would have you without carefulness. He that is unmarried careth for the things that belong to the Lord, how he may please the Lord: <hi type="super">33</hi> But he that is married careth for the things that are of the world, how he may please <hi type="italic">his</hi> wife. 34 There is difference <hi type="italic">also</hi> between a wife and a virgin. The unmarried woman careth for the things of the Lord, that she may be holy both in body and in spirit: but she that is married careth for the things of the world, how she may please <hi type="italic">her</hi> husband. <hi type="super">35</hi> And this I speak for your own profit; not that I may cast a snare upon you, but for that which is comely, and that ye may attend upon the Lord without distraction. <div eID="gen31145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31146" type="x-p"/> The apostle here resumes his discourse, and gives directions to virgins how to act, concerning which we may take notice, <div eID="gen31146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31147" type="x-p"/> I. Of the manner wherein he introduces them: "<hi type="italic">Now concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.25">v. 25</reference>. I have no express and universal law delivered by the Lord himself concerning celibacy; but <hi type="italic">I give my judgment, as one who hath obtained mercy of the Lord to be faithful,</hi>" namely, in the apostleship. He acted faithfully, and therefore his direction was to be regarded as a rule of Christ: for he gave judgment as one who was a faithful apostle of Christ. Though Christ had before delivered no universal law about that matter, he now gives direction by an inspired apostle, one who had obtained mercy of the Lord to be faithful. Note, Faithfulness in the ministry is owing to the grace and mercy of Christ. It is what Paul was ready to acknowledge upon all occasions: <hi type="italic">I laboured more abundantly than they all; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.10">ch. xv. 10</reference>. And it is a great mercy which those obtain from God who prove faithful in the ministry of his word, either ordinary or extraordinary. <div eID="gen31147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31148" type="x-p"/> II. The determination he gives, which, considering the present distress, was that a state of celibacy was preferable: <hi type="italic">It is good for a man so to be,</hi> that is, <hi type="italic">to be single. I suppose,</hi> says the apostle, or it is my opinion. It is worded with modesty, but delivered, notwithstanding, with apostolic authority. It is not the mere opinion of a private man, but the very determination of the Spirit of God in an apostle, though it be thus spoken. And it was thus delivered to give it the more weight. Those that were prejudiced against the apostle might have rejected this advice had it been given with a mere authoritative air. Note, Ministers do not lose their authority by prudent condescensions. They must become all things to all men, that they may do them the more good. <hi type="italic">This is good,</hi> says he, <hi type="italic">for the present distress.</hi> Christians, at the first planting of their religion, were grievously persecuted. Their enemies were very bitter against them, and treated them very cruelly. They were continually liable to be tossed and hurried by persecution. This being the then state of things, he did not think it so advisable for Christians that were single to change conditions. The married state would bring more care and cumber along with it (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.33-1Cor.7.34">v. 33, 34</reference>), and would therefore make persecution more terrible, and render them less able to bear it. Note, Christians, in regulating their conduct, should not barely consider what is lawful in itself, but what may be expedient for them. <div eID="gen31148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31149" type="x-p"/> III. Notwithstanding he thus determines, he is very careful to satisfy them that he does not condemn marriage in the gross, nor declare it unlawful. And therefore, though he says, "If thou <hi type="italic">art loosed from a wife</hi> (in a single state, whether bachelor or widower, virgin or widow) <hi type="italic">do not seek a wife,</hi> do not hastily change conditions;" yet he adds, "<hi type="italic">If thou art bound to a wife, do not seek to be loosed.</hi> It is thy duty to continue in the married relation, and do the duties of it." And though such, if they were called to suffer persecution, would find peculiar difficulties in it; yet, to avoid these difficulties, they must not cast off nor break through the bonds of duty. Duty must be done, and God trusted with events. But to neglect duty is the way to put ourselves out of the divine protection. He adds therefore, <hi type="italic">I thou marry thou hast not sinned; or if a virgin marry she hath not sinned: but such shall have trouble in the flesh.</hi> Marrying is not in itself a sin, but marrying at that time was likely to bring inconvenience upon them, and add to the calamities of the times; and therefore he thought it advisable and expedient that such as could contain should refrain from it; but adds that he would not lay celibacy on them as a yoke, nor, by seeming to urge it too far, draw them into any snare; and therefore says, <hi type="italic">But I spare you.</hi> Note, How opposite in this are the papist casuists to the apostle Paul! They forbid many to marry, and entangle them with vows of celibacy, whether they can bear the yoke or no. <div eID="gen31149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31150" type="x-p"/> IV. He takes this occasion to give general rules to all Christians to carry themselves with a holy indifferency towards the world, and every thing in it. 1. <hi type="italic">As to relations:</hi> Those <hi type="italic">that had wives must be as though they had none;</hi> that is, they must not set their hearts too much on the comforts of the relation; they must be as though they had none. They know not how soon they shall have none. This advice must be carried into every other relation. Those that have children should be as though they had none. Those that are their comfort now may prove their greatest cross. And soon may the flower of all comforts be cut down. 2. As to afflictions: <hi type="italic">Those that weep must be as though they wept not;</hi> that is, we must not be dejected too much with any of our afflictions, nor indulge ourselves in the sorrow of the world, but keep up a holy joy in God in the midst of all our troubles, so that even in sorrow the heart may be joyful, and the end of our grief may be gladness. <hi type="italic">Weeping may endure for a night, but joy will come in the morning.</hi> If we can but get to heaven at last, <hi type="italic">all tears shall be wiped from our eyes;</hi> and the prospect of it now should make us moderate our sorrows and refrain our tears. 3. As to worldly enjoyments: <hi type="italic">Those that rejoice should be as though they rejoiced not;</hi> that is, they should not take too great a complacency in any of their comforts. They must be moderate in their mirth, and sit loose to the enjoyments they most value. Here is not their rest, nor are these things their portion; and therefore their hearts should not be set on them, nor should they place their solace or satisfaction in them. 4. As to worldly traffic and employment: <hi type="italic">Those that buy must be as though they possessed not.</hi> Those that prosper in trade, increase in wealth, and purchase estates, should hold these possessions as though they held them not. It is but setting their hearts on that which is not (<reference osisRef="Prov.23.5">Prov. xxiii. 5</reference>) to do otherwise. Buying and possessing should not too much engage our minds. They hinder many people altogether from minding the better part. Purchasing land and trying oxen kept the guests invited from the wedding-supper, <reference osisRef="Luke.14.18-Luke.14.19">Luke xiv. 18, 19</reference>. And, when they do not altogether hinder men from minding their chief business, they do very much divert them from a close pursuit. Those are most likely to run so as to obtain the prize who ease their minds of all foreign cares and cumbrances. 5. As to all worldly concerns: <hi type="italic">Those that use this world as not abusing it,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.31">v. 31</reference>. The world may be used, but must not be abused. It is abused when it is not used to those purposes for which it is given, to honour God and do good to men—when, instead of being oil to the wheels of our obedience, it is made fuel to lust—when, instead of being a servant, it is made our master, our idol, and has that room in our affections which should be reserved for God. And there is great danger of abusing it in all these respects, if our hearts are too much set upon it. We must keep the world as much as may be out of our hearts, that we may not abuse it when we have it in our hands. <div eID="gen31150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31151" type="x-p"/> V. He enforces these advices with two reasons:—1. <hi type="italic">The time is short,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.29">v. 29</reference>. We have but little time to continue in this world; but a short season for possessing and enjoying worldly things; <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">kairos synestalmenos.</hi></hi> It is contracted, reduced to a narrow compass. It will soon be gone. It is just ready to be wrapped up in eternity. Therefore do not set your hearts on worldly enjoyments. Do not be overwhelmed with worldly cares and troubles. Possess what you must shortly leave without suffering yourselves to be possessed by it. Why should your hearts be much set on what you must quickly resign? 2. <hi type="italic">The fashion of this world passeth away</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.31">v. 31</reference>), <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">schema</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">the habit,</hi> figure, appearance, of the world, passeth away. It is daily changing countenance. It is in a continual flux. It is not so much a world as the appearance of one. All is show, nothing solid in it; and it is transient show too, and will quickly be gone. How proper and powerful an argument is this to enforce the former advice! How irrational is it to be affected with the images, the fading and transient images, of a dream! <hi type="italic">Surely man walketh in a vain show</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.39.6">Ps. xxxix. 6</reference>), in an image, amidst the faint and vanishing appearances of things. And should he be deeply affected, or grievously afflicted, with such a scene? <div eID="gen31151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31152" type="x-p"/> VI. He presses his general advice by warning them against the embarrassment of worldly cares: <hi type="italic">But I would have you without carefulness,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.32">v. 32</reference>. Indeed to be careless is a fault; a wise concern about worldly interests is a duty; but to be careful, full of care, to have an anxious and perplexing care about them, is a sin. All that care which disquiets the mind, and distracts it in the worship of God, is evil; for God must <hi type="italic">be attended upon without distraction,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.35">v. 35</reference>. The whole mind should be engaged when God is worshipped. The work ceases while it diverts to any thing else, or is hurried and drawn hither and thither by foreign affairs and concerns. Those who are engaged in divine worship should attend to this very thing, should make it their whole business. But how is this possible when the mind is swallowed up of the cares of this life? Note, It is the wisdom of a Christian so to order his outward affairs, and choose such a condition in life, as to be without distracting cares, that he may attend upon the Lord with a mind at leisure and disengaged. This is the general maxim by which the apostle would have Christians govern themselves. In the application of it Christian prudence must direct. That condition of life is best for every man which is best for his soul, and keeps him most clear of the cares and snares of the world. By this maxim the apostle solves the case put to him by the Corinthians, whether it were advisable to marry? To this he says, That, by reason of the present distress, and it may be in general, at that time, when Christians were married to infidels, and perhaps under a necessity of being so, if married at all: I say, in these circumstances, to continue unmarried would be the way to free themselves from any cares and incumbrances, and allow them more vacation for the service of God. Ordinarily, the less care we have about the world the more freedom we have for the service of God. Now the married state at that time (if not at all times) did bring most worldly care along with it. <hi type="italic">He that is married careth for the things of the world, that he may please his wife,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.33">v. 33</reference>. <hi type="italic">And she that is married careth for the things of the world, how she may please her husband.</hi> But the unmarried man and woman mind the things of the Lord, that they may please the Lord, and be holy both in body and spirit, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.32">v. 32</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.34">34</reference>. Not but the married person may be holy both in body and spirit too. Celibacy is not in itself a state of greater purity and sanctity than marriage; but the unmarried would be able to make religion more their business at that juncture, because they would have less distraction from worldly cares. Marriage is that condition of life that brings care along with it, though sometimes it brings more than at others. It is the constant care of those in that relation to please each other; though this is more difficult to do at some reasons, and in some cases, than in others. At that season, therefore, the apostle advises that those who were single should abstain from marriage, if they were under no necessity to change conditions. And, where the same reason is plain at other times, the rule is as fit to be observed. And the very same rule must determine persons for marriage where there is the same reason, that is, if in the unmarried state persons are likely to be more distracted in the service of God than if they were married, which is a case supposable in many respects. This is the general rule, which every one's discretion must apply to his own particular case; and by it should he endeavour to determine, whether it be for marriage or against. That condition of life should be chosen by the Christian in which it is most likely he will have the best helps, and the fewest hindrances, in the service of God and the affairs of his own salvation.
entries.8a13ea620d88276579430e314133579752aefd82: <div eID="gen31152" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Prudential Directions to the Unmarried. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31153" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">36</hi> But if any man think that he behaveth himself uncomely toward his virgin, if she pass the flower of <hi type="italic">her</hi> age, and need so require, let him do what he will, he sinneth not: let them marry. <hi type="super">37</hi> Nevertheless he that standeth stedfast in his heart, having no necessity, but hath power over his own will, and hath so decreed in his heart that he will keep his virgin, doeth well. <hi type="super">38</hi> So then he that giveth <hi type="italic">her</hi> in marriage doeth well; but he that giveth <hi type="italic">her</hi> not in marriage doeth better. <div eID="gen31153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31154" type="x-p"/> In this passage the apostle is commonly supposed to give advice about the disposal of children in marriage, upon the principle of his former determination. In this view the general meaning is plain. It was in that age, and those parts of the world, and especially among the Jews, reckoned a disgrace for a woman to remain unmarried past a certain number of years: it gave a suspicion of somewhat that was not for her reputation. "Now," says the apostle, "if any man thinks he behaves unhandsomely towards his daughter, and that it is not for her credit to remain unmarried, when she is of full age, and that upon this principle it is needful to dispose of her in marriage, he may use his pleasure. It is no sin in him to dispose of her to a suitable mate. But if a man has determined in himself to keep her a virgin, and stands to this determination, and is under no necessity to dispose of her in marriage, but is at liberty, with her consent, to pursue his purpose, he does well in keeping her a virgin. In short, he that gives her in marriage does well; but he that keeps her single, if she can be easy and innocent in such a state, does what is better; that is, more convenient for her in the present state of things, if not at all times and seasons." Note, 1. Children should be at the disposal of their parents, and not dispose of themselves in marriage. Yet, 2. Parents should consult their children's inclinations, both to marriage in general and to the person in particular, and not reckon they have uncontrollable power to do with them, and dictate to them, as they please. 3. It is our duty not only to consider what is lawful, but in many cases, at least, what is fit to be done, before we do it. <div eID="gen31154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31155" type="x-p"/> But I think the apostle is here continuing his former discourse, and advising unmarried persons, who are at their own disposal, what to do, the man's virgin being meant of his virginity. <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Terein ten heautou parthenon</hi></hi> seems to be rather meant of preserving his own virginity than keeping his daughter a virgin, though it be altogether uncommon to use the word in this sense. Several other reasons may be seen in Locke and Whitby, by those who will consult them. And it was a common matter of reproach among Jews and civilized heathens, for a man to continue single beyond such a term of years, though all did not agree in limiting the single life to the same term. The general meaning of the apostle is the same, that it was no sin to marry, if a man thought there was a necessity upon, to avoid popular reproach, much less to avoid the hurrying fervours of lust. But he that was in his own power, stood firm in his purpose, and found himself under no necessity to marry, would, at that season, and in the circumstances of Christians at that time, at least, make a choice every way most for his own conveniency, ease, and advantage, as to his spiritual concerns. And it is highly expedient, if not a duty, for Christians to be guided by such a consideration.
entries.f4b36bfaf15834effb5f1e5eb69aab0727f71712: <div eID="gen31155" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Prudential Directions to Widows. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31156" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">39</hi> The wife is bound by the law as long as her husband liveth; but if her husband be dead, she is at liberty to be married to whom she will; only in the Lord. <hi type="super">40</hi> But she is happier if she so abide, after my judgment: and I think also that I have the Spirit of God. <div eID="gen31156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31157" type="x-p"/> The whole is here closed up with advice to widows: <hi type="italic">As long as the husband liveth the wife is bound by the law,</hi> confined to one husband, and bound to continue and cohabit with him. Note, The marriage-contract is for life; death only can annul the bond. <hi type="italic">But, the husband being dead, she is at liberty to marry whom she will.</hi> There is no limitation by God's law to be married only for such a number of times. It is certain, from this passage, that second marriages are not unlawful; for then the widow could not be at liberty to marry whom she pleased, nor to marry a second time at all. But the apostle asserts she has such a liberty, when her husband is dead, only with a limitation that <hi type="italic">she marry in the Lord.</hi> In our choice of relations, and change of conditions, we should always have an eye to God. Note, Marriages are likely to have God's blessing only when they are made in the Lord, when persons are guided by the fear of God, and the laws of God, and act in dependence on the providence of God, in the change and choice of a mate—when they can look up to God, and sincerely seek his direction, and humbly hope for his blessing upon their conduct. <hi type="italic">But she is happier,</hi> says the apostle, <hi type="italic">if she so abide</hi> (that is, continue a widow) <hi type="italic">in my judgment; and I think I have the Spirit of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.40">v. 40</reference>. At this juncture, at least, if not ordinarily, it will be much more for the peace and quiet of such, and give them less hindrance in the service of God, to continue unmarried. And this, he tells them, was by inspiration of the Spirit. "Whatever your false apostles may think of me, I think, and have reason to know, that I have the Spirit of God." Note, Change of condition in marriage is so important a matter that it ought not to be made but upon due deliberation, after careful consideration of circumstances, and upon very probable grounds, at least, that it will be a change to advantage in our spiritual concerns.  <chapter eID="1Cor.7"/> <div eID="gen31157" type="x-p"/>

entries.c1aaf49de92f8460271d46caacad8569f014cd92: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16860"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 7</title> <div sID="gen33257" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.1-1Cor.7.40">1Co 7:1-40</reference>. Reply to Their Inquiries as to Marriage; the General Principle in Other Things Is, Abide in Your Station, for the Time Is Short.<div eID="gen33257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33258" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16860"/>1. The Corinthians in their letter had probably asked questions which tended to disparage marriage, and had implied that it was better to break it off when contracted with an unbeliever.<div eID="gen33258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33259" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">good--</hi>that is, "expedient," because of "the present distress"; that is, the unsettled state of the world, and the likelihood of persecutions tearing rudely asunder those bound by marriage ties. <reference osisRef="Heb.13.4">He 13:4</reference>, in opposition to ascetic and Romish notions of superior sanctity in celibacy, declares, "Marriage is HONORABLE IN ALL." Another reason why in some cases celibacy may be a matter of Christian expediency is stated in <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.34">1Co 7:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.35">35</reference>, "that ye may attend upon the Lord without distraction." But these are exceptional cases, and in exceptional times, such as those of Paul. <div eID="gen33259" type="x-p"/>
entries.66d3f1682d813833b8b9fe87c9bce3be3f631ba0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16861"/><div sID="gen33260" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16861"/>2. Here the general rule is given<div eID="gen33260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33261" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to avoid fornication--</hi>More literally, "on account of fornications," to which as being very prevalent at Corinth, and not even counted sins among the heathen, unmarried persons might be tempted. The plural, "fornications," marks irregular lusts, as contrasted with the unity of the marriage relation [Bengel].<div eID="gen33261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33262" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let every man have--</hi>a positive command to all who have not the gift of continency, in fact to the great majority of the world (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.5">1Co 7:5</reference>). The dignity of marriage is set forth by Paul (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.25-Eph.5.32">Ep 5:25-32</reference>), in the fact that it signifies the mystical union between Christ and the Church. <div eID="gen33262" type="x-p"/>
entries.77729cd7b09226802b28f72e98bdce97f6df4f17: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16862"/><div sID="gen33263" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16862"/>3-4. The duty of cohabitation on the part of the married.<div eID="gen33263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33264" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">due benevolence--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read simply, "her due"; that is, the conjugal cohabitation due by the marriage contract (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.4">1Co 7:4</reference>). <div eID="gen33264" type="x-p"/>
entries.7cf880aea291c85ad40f296b1cda28c773907444: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16864"/><div sID="gen33266" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16864"/><hi type="bold">5. Defraud ... not--</hi>namely, of the conjugal duty "due" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.3">1Co 7:3</reference>; compare the Septuagint, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.10">Ex 21:10</reference>).<div eID="gen33266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33267" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">except it be--</hi>"unless perchance" [Alford].<div eID="gen33267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33268" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">give yourselves to--</hi>literally, "be at leisure for"; be free from interruptions for; namely, on some special "season," as the Greek for "time" means (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.19.15">Ex 19:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.2.16">Joe 2:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.7.3">Zec 7:3</reference>).<div eID="gen33268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33269" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fasting and prayer--</hi>The oldest manuscripts omit "fasting and"; an interpolation, evidently, of ascetics.<div eID="gen33269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33270" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">come together--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "be together," namely, in the regular state of the married.<div eID="gen33270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33271" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Satan--</hi>who often thrusts in his temptations to unholy thoughts amidst the holiest exercises.<div eID="gen33271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33272" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for your incontinency--</hi>because of your inability to "contain" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.9">1Co 7:9</reference>) your natural propensities, which Satan would take advantage of. <div eID="gen33272" type="x-p"/>
entries.8fdb46d6f360bc209d5fd98137510e87ea243334: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16865"/><div sID="gen33273" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16865"/><hi type="bold">6. by permission ... not of commandment--</hi>not by God's permission to me to say it: but, "by way of permission to you, not as a commandment." "This" refers to the directions, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.2-1Cor.7.5">1Co 7:2-5</reference>. <div eID="gen33273" type="x-p"/>
entries.3ef0554a744e223a172d1e9a552602d83c2f8f83: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16866"/><div sID="gen33274" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16866"/><hi type="bold">7. even as I--</hi>having tile gift of continence (<reference osisRef="Matt.19.11">Mt 19:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.19.12">12</reference>). This wish does not hold good absolutely, else the extension of mankind and of the Church would cease; but relatively to "the present distress" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.26">1Co 7:26</reference>). <div eID="gen33274" type="x-p"/>
entries.9ecba860aef9ee5a782166f03d1e33382591c658: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16867"/><div sID="gen33275" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16867"/><hi type="bold">8. to the unmarried--</hi>in general, of both sexes (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.10">1Co 7:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.11">11</reference>).<div eID="gen33275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33276" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and widows--</hi>in particular.<div eID="gen33276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33277" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">even as I--</hi>unmarried (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.5">1Co 9:5</reference>). <div eID="gen33277" type="x-p"/>
entries.119f4303a036ab3d146935cd657bcc75415f654a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16868"/><div sID="gen33278" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16868"/><hi type="bold">9. if they cannot contain--</hi>that is, "have not continency."<div eID="gen33278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33279" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">burn--</hi>with the secret flame of lust, which lays waste the whole inner man. (Compare Augustine [Holy Virginity]). The dew of God's grace is needed to stifle the flame, which otherwise would thrust men at last into hell-fire. <div eID="gen33279" type="x-p"/>
entries.6e4bb51f33df4d77af255141676070052f83bb1b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16869"/><div sID="gen33280" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16869"/><hi type="bold">10. not I, but the Lord--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.12">1Co 7:12</reference>, 25, 40). In ordinary cases he writes on inspired apostolic authority (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.37">1Co 14:37</reference>); but here on the direct authority of the Lord Himself (<reference osisRef="Mark.10.11">Mr 10:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mark.10.12">12</reference>). In both cases alike the things written are inspired by the Spirit of God "but not all for all time, nor all on the primary truths of the faith" [Alford].<div eID="gen33280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33281" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Let not the wife depart--</hi>literally, "be separated from." Probably the separation on either side, whether owing to the husband or to the wife, is forbidden. <div eID="gen33281" type="x-p"/>
entries.13aec48f5d4de0dee1e3aebdf54e87ecae670413: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16870"/><div sID="gen33282" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16870"/><hi type="bold">11. But and if she depart--</hi>or "be separated." If the sin of separation has been committed, that of a new marriage is not to be added (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.32">Mt 5:32</reference>).<div eID="gen33282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33283" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be reconciled--</hi>by appeasing her husband's displeasure, and recovering his good will.<div eID="gen33283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33284" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let not ... husband put away ... wife--</hi>In <reference osisRef="Matt.5.32">Mt 5:32</reference> the only exception allowed is, "saving for the cause of fornication." <div eID="gen33284" type="x-p"/>
entries.77ae5a9a82feb472288891bc351f6076f493c8d9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16871"/><div sID="gen33285" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16871"/><hi type="bold">12. to the rest--</hi>the other classes (besides "the married," <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.10">1Co 7:10</reference>, where both husband and wife are believers) about whom the Corinthians had inquired, namely, those involved in mixed marriages with unbelievers.<div eID="gen33285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33286" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not the Lord--</hi>by any direct command spoken by Him.<div eID="gen33286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33287" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">she be pleased--</hi>Greek, "consents": implying his wish in the first instance, with which hers concurs. <div eID="gen33287" type="x-p"/>
entries.6223893a4e7bc82a2eb1dbde77fc266b1bb70ecf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16872"/><div sID="gen33288" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16872"/><hi type="bold">13. the woman--</hi>a believer.<div eID="gen33288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33289" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let her not leave him--</hi>"her husband," instead of "him," is the reading of the oldest manuscripts The Greek for "leave" is the same as in <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.12">1Co 7:12</reference>, "put away"; translate, "Let her not put away [that is, part with] her husband." The wife had the power of effecting a divorce by Greek and Roman law. <div eID="gen33289" type="x-p"/>
entries.80477fb110870f3654147b535c8113b52fc7932c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16873"/><div sID="gen33290" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16873"/><hi type="bold">14. sanctified--</hi>Those inseparably connected with the people of God are hallowed thereby, so that the latter may retain the connection without impairing their own sanctity (compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.5">1Ti 4:5</reference>); nay, rather imparting to the former externally some degree of their own hallowed character, and so preparing the way for the unbeliever becoming at last sanctified inwardly by faith.<div eID="gen33290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33291" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by ... by--</hi>rather, "in ... in"; that is, in virtue of the marriage tie between them.<div eID="gen33291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33292" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by the husband--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "by the brother." It is the fact of the husband being a "brother," that is, a Christian, though the wife is not so, that sanctifies or hallows the union.<div eID="gen33292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33293" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">else ... children unclean--</hi>that is, beyond the hallowed pale of God's people: in contrast to "holy," that is, all that is within the consecrated limits [Conybeare and Howson]. The phraseology accords with that of the Jews, who regarded the heathen as "unclean," and all of the elect nation as "holy," that is, partakers of the holy covenant. Children were included in the covenant, as God made it not only with Abraham, but with his "seed after" him (<reference osisRef="Gen.17.7">Ge 17:7</reference>). So the faith of one Christian parent gives to the children a near relationship to the Church, just as if both parents were Christians (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.11.16">Ro 11:16</reference>). Timothy, the bearer of this Epistle, is an instance in point (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.1">Ac 16:1</reference>). Paul appeals to the Corinthians as recognizing the principle, that the infants of heathen parents would not be admissible to Christian baptism, because there is no faith on the part of the parents; but where one parent is a believer, the children are regarded as not aliens from, but admissible even in infancy as sharers in, the Christian covenant: for the Church presumes that the believing parent will rear the child in the Christian faith. Infant baptism tacitly superseded infant circumcision, just as the Christian Lord's day gradually superseded the Jewish sabbath, without our having any express command for, or record of, transference. The setting aside of circumcision and of sabbaths in the case of the Gentiles was indeed expressly commanded by the apostles and Paul, but the substitution of infant baptism and of the Lord's day were tacitly adopted, not expressly enacted. No explicit mention of it occurs till Irenæus in the third century; but no society of Christians that we read of disputed its propriety till fifteen hundred years after Christ. Anabaptists would have us defer baptism till maturity as the child cannot understand the nature of it. But a child may be made heir of an estate: it is his, though incapable at the time of using or comprehending its advantage; he is not hereafter to acquire the title and claim to it: he will hereafter understand his claim, and be capable of employing his wealth: he will then, moreover, become responsible for the use he makes of it [Archbishop Whately]. <div eID="gen33293" type="x-p"/>
entries.bb26de118ec406d3737a51c043c2e9e7dfdd3be6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16874"/><div sID="gen33294" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16874"/><hi type="bold">15. if ... depart--</hi>that is, wishes for separation. Translate, "separateth himself": offended with her Christianity, and refusing to live with her unless she renounce it.<div eID="gen33294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33295" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brother or a sister is not under bondage--</hi>is not bound to renounce the faith for the sake of retaining her unbelieving husband [Hammond]. So <reference osisRef="Deut.13.6">De 13:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.10.35-Matt.10.37">Mt 10:35-37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.14.26">Lu 14:26</reference>. The believer does not lie under the same obligation in the case of a union with an unbeliever, as in the case of one with a believer. In the former case he is not bound not to separate, if the unbeliever separate or "depart," in the latter nothing but "fornication" justifies separation [Photius in Æcumenius].<div eID="gen33295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33296" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but God hath called us to peace--</hi>Our Christian calling is one that tends to "peace" (<reference osisRef="Rom.12.18">Ro 12:18</reference>), not quarrelling; therefore the believer should not ordinarily depart from the unbelieving consort (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.12-1Cor.7.14">1Co 7:12-14</reference>), on the one hand; and on the other, in the exceptional case of the unbeliever desiring to depart, the believer is not bound to force the other party to stay in a state of continual discord (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.32">Mt 5:32</reference>). Better still it would be not to enter into such unequal alliances at all (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.40">1Co 7:40</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.14">2Co 6:14</reference>). <div eID="gen33296" type="x-p"/>
entries.a1684beb32045b1d5fba4b41bdb5de3d3cb17275: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16875"/><div sID="gen33297" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16875"/>16. What knowest thou but that by staying with thy unbelieving partner thou mayest save him or her? Enforcing the precept to stay with the unbelieving consort (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.12-1Cor.7.14">1Co 7:12-14</reference>). So Ruth the Moabitess became a convert to her husband's faith: and Joseph and Moses probably gained over their wives. So conversely the unbelieving husband may be won by the believing wife (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.1">1Pe 3:1</reference>) [Calvin]. Or else (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.15">1Co 7:15</reference>), if thy unbelieving consort wishes to depart, let him go, so that thou mayest live "in peace": for thou canst not be sure of converting him, so as to make it obligatory on thee at all costs to stay with him against his will [Menochius and Alford].<div eID="gen33297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33298" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">save--</hi>be the instrument of salvation to (<reference osisRef="Jas.5.20">Jas 5:20</reference>). <div eID="gen33298" type="x-p"/>
entries.20e5940dd0619d9f9efd42feb5505a5d8aabe964: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16876"/><div sID="gen33299" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16876"/><hi type="bold">17. But--</hi>Greek, "If not." "Only." Caution that believers should not make this direction (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.16">1Co 7:16</reference>; as Alford explains it) a ground for separating "of themselves" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.12-1Cor.7.14">1Co 7:12-14</reference>). Or, But if there be no hope of gaining over the unbeliever, still let the general principle be maintained, "As the Lord hath allotted to each, as God hath called each, so let him walk" (so the Greek in the oldest reading); let him walk in the path allotted to him and wherein he was called. The heavenly calling does not set aside our earthly callings.<div eID="gen33299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33300" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">so ordain I in all churches--</hi>Ye also therefore should obey. <div eID="gen33300" type="x-p"/>
entries.9a4a984da694b376855df341101b5eff2a998270: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16877"/><div sID="gen33301" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16877"/><hi type="bold">18. not become uncircumcised--</hi>by surgical operation (1 Maccabees 1:15; Josephus [Antiquities, 12.5.1]). Some Christians in excess of anti-Jewish feeling might be tempted to this.<div eID="gen33301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33302" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let him not be circumcised--</hi>as the Judaizing Christians would have him (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.1">Ac 15:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.5.24">5, 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.5.2">Ga 5:2</reference>). <div eID="gen33302" type="x-p"/>
entries.7a7d1809236e477a342888f9f61d7c91999c43db: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16878"/><div sID="gen33303" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16878"/><hi type="bold">19. Circumcision ... nothing, but ... keeping of ... commandments of God--</hi>namely, is all in all. In <reference osisRef="Gal.5.6">Ga 5:6</reference> this "keeping of the commandments of God" is defined to be "faith which worketh by love"; and in <reference osisRef="Gal.6.15">Ga 6:15</reference>, "a new creature." Circumcision was a commandment of God: but not for ever, as "love." <div eID="gen33303" type="x-p"/>
entries.24ccb819fd2103065f8daecda1240edda78b6ab8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16879"/><div sID="gen33304" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16879"/><hi type="bold">20. the same calling--</hi>that is, the condition from which he is called a Jew, a Greek, a slave, or a freeman. <div eID="gen33304" type="x-p"/>
entries.e1911b9709bb271d186202540e17602871b002d0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16880"/><div sID="gen33305" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16880"/><hi type="bold">21. care not for it--</hi>Let it not be a trouble to thee that thou art a servant or slave.<div eID="gen33305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33306" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">use it rather--</hi>Continue rather in thy state as a servant (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.20">1Co 7:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.3.28">Ga 3:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.2">1Ti 6:2</reference>). The Greek, "But if even thou mayest be made free, use it," and the context (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.20">1Co 7:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.22">22</reference>) favors this view [Chrysostom, Bengel, and Alford]. This advice (if this translation be right) is not absolute, as the spirit of the Gospel is against slavery. What is advised here is, contentment under one's existing condition (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.24">1Co 7:24</reference>), though an undesirable one, since in our union with Christ all outward disparities of condition are compensated (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.22">1Co 7:22</reference>). Be not unduly impatient to cast off "even" thy condition as a servant by unlawful means (<reference osisRef="1Pet.2.13-1Pet.2.18">1Pe 2:13-18</reference>); as, for example, Onesimus did by fleeing (Phm 10-18). The precept (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.23">1Co 7:23</reference>), "Become not (so the Greek) the servants of men," implies plainly that slavery is abnormal (compare <reference osisRef="Lev.25.42">Le 25:42</reference>). "Men stealers," or slave dealers, are classed in <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.10">1Ti 1:10</reference>, with "murderers" and "perjurers." Neander, Grotius, &c., explain, "If called, being a slave, to Christianity, be content--but yet, if also thou canst be free (as a still additional good, which if thou canst not attain, be satisfied without it; but which, if offered to thee, is not to be despised), make use of the opportunity of becoming free, rather than by neglecting it to remain a slave." I prefer this latter view, as more according to the tenor of the Gospel, and fully justified by the Greek. <div eID="gen33306" type="x-p"/>
entries.092c90f239e27d5a9d60671855739fb58c043ecd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16881"/><div sID="gen33307" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16881"/><hi type="bold">22. the Lord's freeman--</hi>(Phm 16)--rather, "freedman." Though a slave externally, spiritually made free by the Lord: from sin, <reference osisRef="John.8.36">Joh 8:36</reference>; from the law, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.2">Ro 8:2</reference>; from "circumcision," <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.19">1Co 7:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.5.1">Ga 5:1</reference>.<div eID="gen33307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33308" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Christ's servant--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.21">1Co 9:21</reference>). Love makes Christ's service perfect freedom (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.29">Mt 11:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.30">30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.5.13">Ga 5:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.16">1Pe 2:16</reference>). <div eID="gen33308" type="x-p"/>
entries.afe4f282ba55a276cdfe0a38c7bc2d1552b8061f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16882"/><div sID="gen33309" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16882"/><hi type="bold">23. be not ye--</hi>Greek, "become not ye." Paul here changes from "thou" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.21">1Co 7:21</reference>) to "ye." Ye all are "bought" with the blood of Christ, whatever be your earthly state (<reference osisRef="1Cor.6.20">1Co 6:20</reference>). "Become not servants to men," either externally, or spiritually; the former sense applying to the free alone: the latter to Christian freemen and slaves alike, that they should not be servile adherents to their party leaders at Corinth (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.21">1Co 3:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.22">22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.23.8-Matt.23.10">Mt 23:8-10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.20">2Co 11:20</reference>); nor indeed slaves to men generally, so far as their condition admits. The external and internal conditions, so far as is attainable, should correspond, and the former be subservient to the latter (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.21">1Co 7:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.32-1Cor.7.35">32-35</reference>). <div eID="gen33309" type="x-p"/>
entries.1894610a2d20b6f9e8f28a46c197ab63bd39d257: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16883"/><div sID="gen33310" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16883"/><hi type="bold">24. abide with God--</hi>being chiefly careful of the footing on which he stands towards God rather than that towards men. This clause, "with God," limits the similar precept in <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.20">1Co 7:20</reference>. A man may cease to "abide in the calling wherein he was called," and yet not violate the precept here. If a man's calling be not favorable to his "abiding with God" (retaining holy fellowship with Him), he may use lawful means to change from it (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.21">1Co 7:21</reference>). <div eID="gen33310" type="x-p"/>
