Now if in other actions of inferior moment no liberty is allowed to children, without the authority of their parents, much less is it reasonable that they should have liberty given them in the contracting of marriage. And that has been carefully enacted by civil law, but more especially by the law of God. So much the more detestable, then, is the wickedness of the Pope, who, laying aside all respect, either for Divine or human laws, has been so daring as to free children from the yoke of subjection to their parents. It is of importance, however, to mark the reason. This, says he, is on account of the dignity of the sacrament. Not to speak of the ignorance of making marriage a sacrament, what honor is there, I beseech you, or what dignity, when, contrary to the general feeling of propriety in all nations, and contrary to God’s eternal appointment, they take off all restraints from the lusts of young persons, that they may, without any feeling of shame, sport themselves, <note n="448"> <div sID="gen118368" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">S’esgayent et desbauchent</foreign>;” — “Sport and debauch themselves.”<div eID="gen118368" type="x-p"/> </note> under pretense of its being a sacrament? Let us know, therefore, that in disposing of children in marriage, the authority of parents is of first-rate importance, provided they do not tyrannically abuse it, as even the civil laws restrict it. <note n="449"> <div sID="gen118369" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Comme aussi a ceste fin les loix ciuiles restraigment l’authorite d’iceux</foreign>;” — “As also for this end civil laws restrict their authority.”<div eID="gen118369" type="x-p"/> </note> The Apostle, too, in requiring exemption from <hi type="italic">necessity</hi>, <note n="450"> <div sID="gen118370" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">En requirant yci que les enfans sentent en eux ceste liberte et exemption de la necessite du mariage</foreign>;” — “In requiring here that children feel in themselves this freedom and exemption from the necessity of marriage.”<div eID="gen118370" type="x-p"/> </note> intimated that the deliberations of parents ought to be regulated with a view to the advantage of their children. Let us bear in mind, therefore, that this limitation is the proper rule — that children allow themselves to be governed by their parents, and that they, on the other hand, do not drag their children by force to what is against their inclination, and that they have no other object in view, in the exercise of their authority, than the advantage of their children.<div eID="gen118367" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.7.37" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen118360" osisID="1Cor.7.37" type="section"/>
entries.12fbd45edf4c8a1b658156fb2260855b83269ffe:
38. Therefore he that giveth in marriage. Here we have the conclusion from both parts of the statement, in which he states, in a few words, that parents are free from blame if they give away their daughters in marriage, while he at the same time declares that they do better if they keep them at home unmarried. You are not, however, to understand that celibacy is here preferred to marriage, otherwise than under the exception which was a little before expressed. For if power be wanting on the part of the daughter,
“Car quand la puissance defaudra a la fille de s’abstenir de mariage;” — “For when the daughter has not power to abstain from marriage.”
the father acts an exceedingly bad part if he endeavors to keep her back from marriage, and would be no longer a father to her, but a cruel tyrant. The sum of the whole discussion amounts to this — that celibacy is better than marriage, because it has more liberty, so that persons can serve God with greater freedom; but at the same time, that no necessity ought to be imposed, so as to make it unlawful for individuals to marry, if they think proper; and farther, that marriage itself is a remedy appointed by God for our infirmity,
“Pour subuenir a nostre infirmite;” — “To help our infirmity.”
which all ought to use that are not endowed with the gift of continency. Every person of sound judgment will join with me in acknowledging and confessing, that the whole of Paul’s doctrine on this point is comprehended in these three articles.
1 Corinthians 7:39-40
39. The wife is bound by the law as long as her husband liveth; but if her husband be dead, she is at liberty to be married to whom she will; only in the Lord.
39. Muller alligata est Legi, quamdiu maritus ejus vivit: si auterm dormierit maritus ejus, libera est, ut cui vult nubat, modo in Domino.
40. But she is happier if she so abide, after my judgment: and I think also that I have the Spirit of God.
40. Beatior vero est, si sic maneat,secundum meam sententiam: existimo autem, me quoque Spiritum Dei habere.
entries.3838c18f8862446f5b0223e08e87b2d9255dd31b: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.7.39" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.7.39" sID="gen118382" type="section"/> <div sID="gen118383" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">39.</hi> <hi type="italic">The wife is bound</hi> He had previously spoken indiscriminately of husbands and wives, but as wives, on account of the modesty of their sex, might seem to have less liberty, he has thought it necessary to give in addition some special directions in reference to them. He now, therefore, teaches that women are not less at liberty than men to marry a second time, on their becoming widows. <note n="453"> <div sID="gen118384" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Apres auoir perdu lears premiers maris</foreign>;” — “After having lost their first husbands.”<div eID="gen118384" type="x-p"/> </note> We have already mentioned above, that those who desired a second marriage were branded with the reproach of intemperance, and that, with the view of putting some kind of slight upon them, those who had been contented with being once married, were wont to be presented with the “chaplet of chastity.” Nay more, this first opinion had, in course of time, become prevalent among Christians; for second marriages had no blessing pronounced upon them, and some Councils prohibited the clergy from being present on such occasions. The Apostle here condemns tyranny of that sort, and declares, that no hindrance ought to be thrown in the way of widows’ marrying, if they think proper.<div eID="gen118383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen118385" type="x-p"/>It is of little consequence, and so far as the sense is concerned it matters nothing, whether we say that the wife is bound <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">legi</hi></foreign>, (<hi type="italic">to </hi>the law,) in the dative, or <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">lege</hi></foreign>, (<hi type="italic">by </hi>the law,) in the ablative. For it is the law that declares the connection between husband and wife to be indissoluble. If, however, you read it in the dative, the term will convey the idea of authority or obligation. <note n="454"> <div sID="gen118386" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Authoritc ou puissance et suiection</foreign>;” — “Authority or power and subjection.”<div eID="gen118386" type="x-p"/> </note> Now he reasons from contraries; for if a woman is bound to her husband for life, she is, then, set at liberty by his death. After she has been set at liberty, <hi type="italic">let her be married to whom she will</hi><div eID="gen118385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen118387" type="x-p"/>When the verb <hi type="italic">to sleep</hi> means <hi type="italic">to die</hi>, <note n="455"> <div sID="gen118388" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Comme en ce passage</foreign>;” — “As in this passage.”<div eID="gen118388" type="x-p"/> </note> it refers not to the soul, but to the body, as is manifest from its constant use in Scripture. <note n="456"> <div sID="gen118389" type="x-p"/> The original expression is <foreign xml:lang="el">ἐὰν δὲ κοιμηθὟ ὁ ἀνὴρ αὐτὢς</foreign>, — “If her husband has <hi type="italic">fallen asleep</hi>.” The metaphor is not peculiar to the Scriptures, but is made use of also by heathen writers, of which we have a beautiful instance in Callimachus — <foreign xml:lang="el">ἱερον ὑπνον Κοιμαται· Θνησκειν μη λεγε τους αγαθους· </foreign><hi type="italic">He sleeps a sacred sleep</hi> — <hi type="italic">say not that good men die</hi>. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen118389" type="x-p"/> </note> It is a foolish part, therefore, that is acted by certain fanatics, who, from this little word, make it their endeavor to prove that the souls of men, after being separated from their bodies, are destitute of thought and intelligence, or, in other words, of their life.<div eID="gen118387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen118390" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Only in the Lord</hi> This is thought to be added for the purpose of admonishing them in passing, that they ought not to yoke themselves with the irreligious, or to covet their society. This, I acknowledge, is true, but I am of opinion that more is meant that they should do this in a religious way, and in the fear of the Lord, <note n="457"> <div sID="gen118391" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Auce reuerence, sagement, et en la erainte du Seigneur</foreign>;” — “With reverence, wisely, and in the fear of the Lord.”<div eID="gen118391" type="x-p"/> </note> for it is in this manner that marriages are formed auspiciously.<div eID="gen118390" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.7.39" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen118382" osisID="1Cor.7.39" type="section"/>
entries.40ada05ee26532c636a7d0842ac267574332aeb3:
40. But she is happier if she so abide Why? Is it because widowhood is of itself a virtue? No; but because it will have less to distract, and is more exempt from earthly cares. As to what he adds — according to my judgment, he does not mean by this expression that his opinion was doubtful; but it is as if he had said that such was his decision as to this question; for he immediately adds that he has the Spirit of God, which is sufficient to give full and perfect authority. There appears, at the same time, to be somewhat of irony when he says I think For as the false apostles were ever and anon boasting in high-sounding terms of their having the Spirit of God, for the purpose of arrogating to themselves authority, and in the meantime endeavored to derogate from that of Paul, he says that he thinks that he is not less a partaker of the Spirit than they
CHAPTER 8
1 Corinthians 8:1-7
1. Now as touching things offered unto idols, we know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth.
1. De iis porro quae idolis immolantur, scimus, quod omnes scientiam habemus: scientia inflat, caritas autem aedificat.
2. And if any man think that he knoweth any thing, he knoweth nothing yet as he ought to know.
2. Si quis autem videtur sibi aliquid scire, nondum quicquam scit,qualiter scire oportet.
3. But if any man love God, the same is known of him.
3. At si quis diligit Deum, hie cognitus est ab illo.
4. As concerning therefore the eating of those things that are offered in sacrifice unto idols, we know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is none other God but one.
4. De esu ergo eorum quae idolis immolantur, novimus, quod idolum nihil est in mundo, et quod non est alius Deus nisi unus.
5. For though there be that are called gods, whether in heaven or in earth, (as there be gods many, and lords many,)
5. Nam etsi sunt qui vocentur dii, sire in coelo sive super terram, quemadmodum sunt dii multi et domini multi:
6. But to us there is but one God, the Father, of whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things, and we by him.
6. Nobis tamen unus Deus Pater, ex quo omnia, et nos in ipso: et unus Dominus Iesus Christus, per quem omnia, et nos per ipsum.
7. Howbeit there is not in every man that knowledge: for some with conscience of the idol unto this hour eat it as a thing offered unto an idol; and their conscience being weak is defiled.
7. At non est in omnibus scientia: quidam autem cum idoli conscientia nunc quoque tanquam idolo immolatum edunt, et conscientia eorum, infirma quum sit, polluitur.

entries.4011a24d53e9616165e3c1e0c395ad99babfd5d7:
<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="7" type="chapter">
               <ns0:head>CHAP. VII.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p n="1">1 NOw concerning the things whereof ye wrote unto me <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">It seemeth, that though this Church was very much cor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rupted, yet some of them retained a reverence for this great Apostle, and had wrote one or more Letters to him about some points, to which he returneth answer.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>It is</ns0:hi> good for a man not to touch a woman <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">It seemeth that one thing they had wrote to him about, was about Marriage, not about the lawfulness of marrying (that Doctrine of Devils was not broached so early in the World) but concerning the advisa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bleness of marriage, and mens use of their wives in that afflicted state of the Church.</ns0:note>.<ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">The Apostle answereth, <ns0:hi>That it is good for a man not to touch a woman.</ns0:hi> When he saith, it is <ns0:hi>good,</ns0:hi> he means only more convenient or better, with respect to the troubled state of the Church, or that persons might be more at liberty for the service of God and the duties of Religion. Upon these accouts it were more convenient for a man not to marry (for that he meaneth by <ns0:hi>touching a woman.</ns0:hi>)</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 Nevertheless <ns0:hi>to avoid</ns0:hi> fornication, let every man have his own wife, and let every woman have her own husband <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">In the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> it is, <ns0:hi>because of fornications</ns0:hi>; the sense of which can be no other than this which our Translators give. The word is in the <ns0:hi>Plural number,</ns0:hi> to signifie that that which he mean<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth by this term, is all sorts of impurities and uncleannesses, which are the products of the <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>usts of the flesh. These are sins of that nature and <ns0:hi>species,</ns0:hi> that if we cannot chuse what in re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spect of some circumstances would be more convenient, we must baulk it, rather than run into such a guilt. The Apostle doth therefore determine that in this case, it was every mans duty to marry, and every womans likewise; the reason of which must be, because God had ordained marriage as a means to bridle men, and restrain them from extravagant lusts. [His own wife] [her own husband] a clear place against Polygamy.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Pet. 3.7.</ns0:note> Let the husband render unto the wife due benevolence <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">The word translated <ns0:hi>due benevolence,</ns0:hi> signifieth due good will or kindness, but from <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 5. it appeareth what the Apostle meaneth; <ns0:hi>Moses, Exod.</ns0:hi> 21.10. calleth it, <ns0:hi>the duty of marriage,</ns0:hi> both of them using a modest term in expressing the conjugal act, as we shall observe the Scripture always doing, when there is occasion to mention what men of profane hearts are ready to make a scoff at.</ns0:note>: and likewise also the wife unto the husband <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">The Apostle maketh this the mutual duty both of husband and wife under due circumstances, therefore useth the word <ns0:hi>render,</ns0:hi> which implieth the thing required to be an act of justice.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 The wife hath not power of her own body, but the husband: likewise also the husband hath not power over his own body, but the wife <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">He gives the reason of it, because marriage takes away from each married person the power over his or her own body, and giveth it to their correlate. The Apostle seemeth here to an<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />swer a question propounded to him by some Members of this Church: Whether, though they were married, the husband and wife might not forbear each others bed, and make use of their society each with other meerly for helps in other things, such as getting an Estate, looking after the affairs of a Family, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> which the Apostle doth by no means judge advisable.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Joel 2.16.</ns0:note> Defraud not one another <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">That is, withhold not your selves one from another, which he rightly calls defrauding one another, because he had before declared it a debt; and further declared, that neither the hus<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />band nor the wife had a power over their own bodies, but the power of either of their bodies was in their correlate.</ns0:note>, except <ns0:hi>it be</ns0:hi> with consent <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">He adds, <ns0:hi>except it be with consent,</ns0:hi> mutual consent, and then it is indeed no defrauding.</ns0:note> for a time, that ye may give your selves to fasting and prayer <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">And <ns0:hi>for a time,</ns0:hi> for a religious end, that they might give themselves to Fasting and Prayer, not that this abstinence is necessary to us by any Divine precept, to prepare us for solemn Prayer, (for such only is here spoken of) for then the Apostle would not have made consent necessary in this case, but the Jews were commanded it, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 19.15. as a prepara<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion to their hearing of the Law, and it was a plece of the legal purification, as appeareth from 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 21.4. as to which Chri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stians were at liberty, and might observe or not observe it, as they agreed.</ns0:note>, and come together again <ns0:hi>k,</ns0:hi> that Satan tempt you not for your incontinency <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Then he requires, that they should return to their former course, not defrauding one another, lest the Devil observing their abstinence, should tempt them to unlawful mix<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tures, seeing their inability to contain themselves within the bounds of temperance and chastity.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 But I speak this by permission, and not of commandment <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Some refer these words to all that had gone before in this <ns0:hi>Chapter</ns0:hi>; but the best Interpreters rather refer them to what went immediately before in the preceding verse, declaring, that he had no express command from God, as to those things of ab<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />staining for a time for <ns0:hi>Fasting and Prayer,</ns0:hi> and then <ns0:hi>coming toge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther again,</ns0:hi> but he spake what he judged equitable and reasona<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble; but as to particular persons, they ought to judge and govern themselves according to their particular circumstances.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 For <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Acts 26.29.</ns0:note> I would that all men were even as I my self <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>I would,</ns0:hi> in this place can signifie no more, than I could wish or desire (if it were the will of God) that all Christians had the gift of continency, which God (blessed be his Name) hath given me: that this is meant, is plain by the next words, and <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 9. it is apparent, that <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> did not will this absolutely; for that had been to have willed the disolution of the World, as well as the Church, within the compass of that Age.</ns0:note>: but <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 12.1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                  </ns0:note> every man hath his proper gift of God, one after this manner, and another after that <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">But, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>aith the Apostle, every one hath not the gift of continency, one hath it, another hath it not, which is the same thing which our Saviour said in reply to his Disciples, saying, <ns0:hi>If the case of the man <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e so with his wife, it is not good to marry,</ns0:hi> Matt. 19.10. <ns0:hi>All men cannot receive this saying, save they to whom it is given.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 I say therefore to the unmarried and widows, It is good for them if they abide even as I <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">By the unmarried and widows, it is apparent that <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> means Virgins that were never married, and such as having been once married, had lost their husbands, though the first word in the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> had been significa<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ive enough of persons in both these states; yet the Apostle<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>sing of two words, makes it past dispute, when he saith, <ns0:hi>It is good for such</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>be as he was</ns0:hi>; his meaning is, that it was better with respect to the present circumstances of Christians, or <ns0:hi>it was convenient,</ns0:hi> in which notion good is often taken, not for what is absolutely good, and indeed the nature of all good lyeth in the conveniency or suitableness of the thing so called to us; and though in the Di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vine precepts there is always such a suitableness, so as they must be always good, yet in other things, which God hath le<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>t to our liberty (such as is this of marriage) a thing may be <ns0:hi>good</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>evil,</ns0:hi> as the circumstances of several persons, yea, of the same person, may vary. S. <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> considereth only the circumstances of the World common to all Christians, and upon them deter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mines this goodness, supposing the circumstances of the parti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cular person not to rule otherwise. His not saying, <ns0:hi>It is good for them not to marry,</ns0:hi> but to be as he was, hath bred a question of no great import to be determined, whether <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> was ever married or no, in the determination of which the <ns0:hi>Ancients</ns0:hi> cou<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>d not agree: but it is not worth spending our time about, con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sidering that all agree, he was at this time unmarried, which is all he doth here mean: if S. <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> was never married, we are sure <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> was; for we read of his <ns0:hi>wifes mother sick of a feav<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>r, Mark</ns0:hi> 1.30.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:442" />9 But <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Ti<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 5.14.</ns0:note> if they cannot contain, let them mar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry: <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">That S. <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi>'s saying, <ns0:hi>It is good,</ns0:hi> &c. did not signifie it is the will of God, or (as the <ns0:hi>Papists</ns0:hi> would have it) it is my counsel in order to your further perfection, is plain by his pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cept for them to marry, if they could not contain; and this likewise lets us see that <ns0:hi>second Marriages</ns0:hi> are not only lawful, but may be an incumbent duty, that is, if they who are concerned as to them, cannot contain themselves within the bounds and rule of chastity, which must not only be interpreted with refe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rence to acts of Uncleanness.</ns0:note> for it is better to marry then to burn <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">This is contradicted by the reason given by the Apostle, determining that marriage was much more <ns0:hi>eligible</ns0:hi> than <ns0:hi>burning,</ns0:hi> which term signifies the in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ward fervor and eager inclinations of the mind, not the acts only of the outward man.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 And unto the married I command, <ns0:hi>yet</ns0:hi> not I, but the Lord <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 2.14. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.32. & 1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.6. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 10.11. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 16.1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note>, Let not the wife depart from <ns0:hi>her</ns0:hi> husband <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">The Apostle had spoke to married before, but in ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther case, he now returneth in his discourse to them again, speaking to another case, which it should seem they had put to him, what it was is not plainly expressed, but it may easily be gathered from <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 12, 13. as also from the Apostles determi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nation in this verse: it was this, <ns0:hi>Whether it was lawful for the husband or the wi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e depart from his wi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e, or her husband,</ns0:hi> unless it were in the case of <ns0:hi>Adultery</ns0:hi>; for though here be nothing spoken as to that case, yet it plainly must be accepted, as de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />termined before by our Saviour; but as the Jews, so the Hea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thens amongst whom these <ns0:hi>Corinthians</ns0:hi> lived, had entertained much too mean thoughts about the Marriage-bond, indulging themselves in a liberty to break it for every slight cause, and it should seem by <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 12, 13. it was judged by them a sufficient cause, if one of them were not converted to the Faith of Christ. Now in this case, saith the Apostle, I <ns0:hi>command,</ns0:hi> and what I tell you is the Will of God, it is not I alone who command it, but you are to look upon it as the Will of God concerning you, though revealed to you by me that am the Minister of God to you.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Let not the wi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e depart from her husband:</ns0:hi> she may be divorced from her husband in case of fornication, but let her not for any other cause make a voluntary secession.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 But and if she depart <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">How our Translators came to translate <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, which is manifestly a <ns0:hi>Verb Passive</ns0:hi> [<ns0:hi>if she depart</ns0:hi>] I cannot tell. It signi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fieth, if she be departed, and so is as well significative of a be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing parted from her husband by a judicial act of Divorce, as of a <ns0:hi>voluntary departing.</ns0:hi> The Jews were wont to give Bills of Divorce to their wives, for any trivial cause. The word is to be interpreted as well of any <ns0:hi>legal Divorce,</ns0:hi> not according to the true meaning of the Divine Law, as concerning a volun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tary secession: in which case the Apostle commandeth,</ns0:note>, let her remain un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />married <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">that she should marry to no other; the reason is plain, because no such cause to divorce broke the bond of marriage, she was yet the wife of her former husband in Gods eye and account, and committed adultery, if she married to another, as our Saviour had determined, <ns0:hi>Matt.</ns0:hi> 5.32. & 19.9.</ns0:note>, or be reco<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                     <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                  </ns0:gap>ciled to <ns0:hi>her</ns0:hi> husband <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">but he gives her a li<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="3 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>•••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ty to be reconciled to her husband. In case that a woman put away by her husband, became another mans wife, by the Law, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 24.4. she might not (though that latter husband died) return to her former husband; but in case she remained unmarried, she might be reconciled to him.</ns0:note>: and let not the husband put away <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> wife <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">The Apostle giveth the same precept concerning husbands.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 But to the rest speak I, not the Lord <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Either as to the other part of your Epistle, or as to the cases of the rest mentioned in your Epistle, I shall give you my advice so far as I am instructed by the holy Spirit of God, though our Lord Jesus Christ hath set no certain rule concern<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing them.</ns0:note>, If any brother hath a wife that believeth not <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>That believeth not,</ns0:hi> both in this and <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 13. signi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fieth, that hath not embraced the Christian Faith, but still re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />maineth a Pagan.</ns0:note>, and she be pleased to dwell with him <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">If there be no other matter of difference betwixt such persons, save only in matter of Religion,</ns0:note>, let him not put her away <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">let him not for that put her away. If a Christian man or woman had their choice to make, it were unlawful for either of them to make choice of a <ns0:hi>Pagan</ns0:hi> for their yoke-fellow: but if after mar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />riage either the husband or the wife embraceth the Christian Faith, the other correlate still abiding a <ns0:hi>Pagan,</ns0:hi> their difference in Religion is not a sufficient ground for a separation, this seem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth to be the Apostles meaning. The case seemeth a little different in the opinion of some Divines, when the <ns0:hi>Idolater</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Idolatress blasphemeth God</ns0:hi> and the true Religion, and is conti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nually tempting the correlate to Apostasie: but it is hard to determine against the plain precept of so great an Apostle, especially considering the reason by which he backeth his pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cept.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 And the woman which hath an husband that believeth not, and if he be pleased to dwell with her, let her not leave him.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 For the unbelieving husband is sanctified <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Sanctifying in holy Writing generally signifieth the separa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion, or setting apart of a person or thing from a common, to, and for an holy use, whether it be by some external Rites and Ceremonies, or by the infusing of some inward spiritual habits. In this place it seemeth to have a different sense from what it usually hath in holy Writ; for it can neither signifie the sancti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fication of the person by in<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>used habits of Grace; for nei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther is the unbelieving husband thus sanctified by the believing wi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>e, neither is the unbelieving wife thus sanctified by the be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lieving husband. Nor are either of them thus set apart for the service of God by any legal Rites, which hath made a great dif<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ference in the notions of Interpreters, how the unbelieving husband is sanctified by the believing wife, or the unbelieving wife by the believing husband. Some think it signifies no more than <ns0:hi>prepared for God,</ns0:hi> as sanctified signifies, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 13.3. Others think they are <ns0:hi>sanctified</ns0:hi> by a moral denomination, I rather think it signifies <ns0:hi>brought into such a state, that the Believer, without offence to the Law of God, may continue in a married estate with such a yoke-fellow:</ns0:hi> and the state of marriage is an holy state, notwithstanding the disparity with reference to Religion.</ns0:note> by the wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified by the husband; Else were your children unclean <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">O<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />therwise he saith, the <ns0:hi>children</ns0:hi> begotten and born of such pa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rents would be <ns0:hi>unclean,</ns0:hi> in the same state that the children of <ns0:hi>Pagan</ns0:hi> parents are without the Church, not within the Cove<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nant, not under the Promise. In one sense all children are un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />clean, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> children of wrath, born in sin, and brought forth in iniquity; but all are not in this sense <ns0:hi>unclean,</ns0:hi> some are with<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />in the Covenant of Grace, within the Church, capable of Ba<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ptism.</ns0:note>, but now they are holy <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">These are those that are called holy, not as inward<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly renewed and sanctified, but relatively, in the same sense that all the Jewish Nation are called an <ns0:hi>holy people</ns0:hi>; and pos<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sibly this may give us a further light to understand the term <ns0:hi>sanctified,</ns0:hi> in the former part of the verse. The unbelieving husband is so far sanctified by the believing wife, and the unbe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lieving wife so far sanctified by the believing husband, that as they may lawfully continue in their married relation, and live together as man and wife, so the issue coming from them both shall he by God counted in Covenant with him, and have a right to Baptism, which is one of the Seals of that Covenant, as well as those children both whose parents are Believers.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 But if the unbelieving depart, let him de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />part <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">If the unbelieving husband, or the unbelieving wife will leave his or her correlate, that is, so leave them, as to return no more to live as an husband, or as a wife with her or him that is Christian, let him depart. Such a person hath broken the bond of marriage, and in such cases Christians are not un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der bondage, they are not tyed by Law to fetch them again, nor by the Laws of God to keep themselves unmarried for their perverseness. But it <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ay be objected, That nothing but <ns0:hi>Adul<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tery</ns0:hi> by t<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>e <ns0:hi>Divine Law</ns0:hi> breaketh that bond. <ns0:hi>Answ.</ns0:hi> That is de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nied. Nothing but <ns0:hi>Adultery</ns0:hi> is a justifiable cause of divorce. No man may put away his wife, nor any wife put away her hus<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />band but for <ns0:hi>Adultery.</ns0:hi> But the husbands voluntary leaving his wife, or the wi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>es voluntary leaving her husband, with a reso<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lution to return no more to them, breaks also the bond of mar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />riage, frustrating it as to the ends for which God hath appointed it, and after all due means used, to bring again the party de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />parting, to their duty, doth certainly free the correlate. So that although nothing can justifie repudiation or putting away a wife or an husband, and marrying another, but the adultery of the person so divorced and repudiated, yet the departure either of husband and wife without the others consent for a long time, and refusal to return after all due means used, especially if the party so go<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ng away, doth it out of an hatred and abo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mination of the others Religion, will justifie the person so de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />serted after due waiting and use of means to reduce him or her to their duty, wholly to cast off the person deserting, for no Christian in such case by Gods Law is under bondage.</ns0:note>. A brother or a sister is not under bondage in such <ns0:hi>cases g:</ns0:hi> but God hath called us <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Gr, <ns0:hi>in peace.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> to peace <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">For God hath called Christians unto peace, and in his ordinance of marriage aimed at the quiet and peace of his people in their se<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>vice of him in their families and relations; and therefore as Christians ought not to disturb the peace of their own conscien<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ces, turning away their relations, though they be Unbelievers: yet neither are they bound, if such will leave them, to court their own continual trouble and disturbance.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:443" />16 For what knowest thou, O wife, whether thou shalt <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Pet. 3.1.</ns0:note> save <ns0:hi>thy</ns0:hi> husband? or how knowest thou, O man, whether thou shalt save <ns0:hi>thy</ns0:hi> wife? <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">The Apostle having before determined the lawfulness of a Christian husbands or wifes abiding in a state of marriage with a wife or husband that was an infidel, if she or he were willing to abide with the Believer, now argues the great advantage which might be from it, for the glory of God, and the good of the Soul of such husband or wife: <ns0:hi>What knowest thou, O wife</ns0:hi> (saith he) it is not certain, that God will so far bless thy con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />verse with thy husband or wife, as that thou shalt, by thy in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />struction, admonition, or example, be an occasion or instru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment to bring them to Christ; but it is neither impossible nor improbable, and their willingness (notwithstanding their diffe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rence from thee in Religion, yet) to abide with thee, may give thee some hopes that they will hearken to thee. They are often (in the language of holy Writ) said, to <ns0:hi>save others,</ns0:hi> who are instrumental to bring them to Christ, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 9.22. 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 4.16. <ns0:hi>Iam.</ns0:hi> 5.20. We ought to bear with many inconveni<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ences to our selves, where our bearing with them may any way promote the glory of God, or the good of Souls.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 But as God hath distributed to every man, as the Lord hath called <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Calling</ns0:hi> in this place signifieth that station and course of life, wherein by the Providence of God any man is set. Some think, that this precept hath a special reference to what went before, as if the sense were this, If God by his Providence hath so ordered it that thy heart be changed, thy wifes or thy hus<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bands heart being not yet changed, but he or she remaining Pagans, yet let not this cause any separation betwixt you, but, unless the Unbeliever will depart, live yet as man and wife to<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gether, mutually performing conjugal offices each to other. But the following verses where the Apostle, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 21. speaks of <ns0:hi>Calling</ns0:hi> being a servant, shew this interpretation to be too narrow. The sense of the Text is: That the Profession of Christianity is con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sistent with any honest calling or course of life, and it is the will of God that Christians should not pretend their profession of Religion, to excuse them from the duties of any relation wherein they are set. This is an universal Rule,</ns0:note> every one, so let him walk: And so ordain I in all churches <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">and con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cerned not the Church of <ns0:hi>Corinth</ns0:hi> only, but all other Churches of Christ, being an Apostolical Constitution.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 Is any man called being circumcised? let him not become uncircumcised: Is any called in uncir<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cumcision? let him not become circumcised <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Is any one who was a native Jew, and so circumcised ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cording to the Jewish Law converted (while he is in that state) to the Faith of Christ, let him not affect the state of him, that having been formerly a <ns0:hi>Gentile,</ns0:hi> was never circumcised. On the other side, is any, being a native Gentile, and so not circum<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cised, converted to Christianity, let not him affect the state of one converted from Judaism, who was circumcised. This is doubtless the sense of the verse, not (as some would have it) let him not endeavour by art to make himself uncircumcised, which was the wicked practice of some (for a better compli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ance with the Gentiles) of whom we read, 1 <ns0:hi>Maccab.</ns0:hi> 1.17.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gal. 6.15.</ns0:note> Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sion is nothing <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Circumcision was an Ordinance of God, a sign of Gods Covenant, as necessary to Salvation in its time, as the fulfilling of any precept of the Law contained in Ordinances: and Un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />circumcision also was something; for by the Law relating to that Ordinance, the uncircumcised male is determined to have broken Gods Covenant, and determined to a cutting off, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 17.10, 11, 12, 13, 14.</ns0:note>, but the keeping the command<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments of God <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">But in the present state of the Church, Circumcision wa<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> of no value or moment in the business of Sal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vation: <ns0:hi>Gal</ns0:hi> 5.6. <ns0:hi>In Christ Iesus neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision, but <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>aith which worketh by love.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 Let every man abide in the same calling wherein he was called <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Let every man abide in the same state and condition of life in which he was when he was first converted to the Faith of Christ, that is, supposing that he was in an honest course of life (for we read that the Conjurers in the <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> burnt their books, and unlawful courses of life must not be adhered to after men have once given up their names to Christ.) The Apostles design is only to shew, that the Profession of Christianity maketh no state of life unlawful, which was before that profession lawful, nor dischargeth any from such as were before the duties of persons in their circumstances and relations. They too far strain this Text who interpret it into an obligation upon all men, not to alter that particular way and course of life and trading, to which they were educated, and in which they formerly have been in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gaged, though such a thing be of too great moment and conse<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quence for any to do without just advice and deliberation. The world is a mutable thing, and trades and particular courses of life wear out, and what will now bring in a due livelihood, pos<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sibly seven years hence will not furnish any with bread, and 'tis unreasonable in such a case to think, that the Rule of Christian profession tyes up a man under these changes of Providence to such a particular course of life, as he cannot in it, <ns0:hi>in the sweat of his face eat his bread.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 Art thou called <ns0:hi>being</ns0:hi> a servant <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">If whiles thou art a servant to another in any honest im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ployment, thou art converted to the Christian Religion, let it not trouble thee, matter it not. A man may be the servant of Christ, and yet a servant to men in any honest imployment.</ns0:note>? care not for it: but if thou mayst be made free, use <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> ra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>But if thou mayst be made free</ns0:hi> by the favour of thy friends with the consent of thy master, <ns0:hi>use it rather,</ns0:hi> that is, (say some) ra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther chuse to be a servant still (which indeed in some cases may be the duty of a good Christian) that is, if thou seest, that in that station thou canst better serve God and the interest of thy masters or other Souls. But it is more probable the sense is, make use of thy liberty rather: for certain it is, that the free<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />man is ordinarily at more advantage for the service of God than he that is a servant.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 For he that is called in the Lord, <ns0:hi>being</ns0:hi> a ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vant <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Joh. 8.36<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Rom. 6.18, 2<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                  </ns0:note>, is the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Gr. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 span">
                        <ns0:desc>〈…〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> Lords free-man: likewise also he that is called <ns0:hi>being</ns0:hi> free, is <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 9.21. Gal. 5.13. Eph. 6.6. 1 Pet. 2.16.</ns0:note> Christs servant <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">For the state of a servant to men, no way prejudiceth <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> man as to his spiritual liberty: a servant and a free-man consi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dered with reference to Christ, are both one; a servant may be as near the Kingdom of Heaven as a free-man, and let a man be in never so good a state of civil liberty; yet if he be a Christian, he is still a servant of Christ, and bound in all things to obey him. As to the <ns0:hi>new man,</ns0:hi> there is <ns0:hi>neither bond nor free, but Christ is all and in all.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 6.20. 1 Pet. 1.18, 19.</ns0:note> Ye are bought with a price, be not ye the servants of men <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">What price we are bought with, we heard <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 6.20. the Apostle there pressed it upon us as our duty to glorifie God with our bodies and our spirits: here he presseth upon us ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther duty, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> upon that consideration not to be <ns0:hi>the servants of men:</ns0:hi> by which some think he forbiddeth the selling themselves as slaves to Infidels: others think that he only forbiddeth <ns0:hi>eye-service,</ns0:hi> as the Apostle calls it, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 6.6. while in the mean time they might be the servants of men, if they served them <ns0:hi>as the ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart, with good will doing service as to the Lord, not to men.</ns0:hi> But the most probable in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />terpretation is, Be not servants to the lusts of men, wherein you can serve men, and in the same actions also serve God, and be obedient to his Will: you may be the servants of men, but be not servants of men in such actions wherein to serve them, you must disobey God.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 Brethren, let every man wherein he is cal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led, therein abide with God <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">In whatsoever state or condition, whether he be married or unmarried, whether he be a master or a servant, whether he were before circumcised or uncircumcised, let him not think Christianity obligeth him to alter it, he may abide in it, only he must abide in it <ns0:hi>with God,</ns0:hi> as one who remembreth Gods Eye is upon him, and seeth him, and that he is bound to ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />prove himself in it unto God, and to keep a good conscience towards him, as one that is a Member of the Church of God, and under the Laws of it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25 Now concerning virgins <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">He had before spoken to married persons and widows, now he comes to speak concerning Virgins; and though <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>e mentions only the <ns0:hi>female Sex,</ns0:hi> yet the following words shew that his advice extended to both.</ns0:note>, I have no com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mandment of the Lord <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">As to them he saith, he had no special direction from Christ, none that would suit the case of every Virgin,</ns0:note>: yet I give my judg<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">but ye<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> he would give his advice, wh<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> seemed to him best.</ns0:note>, as one that hath obtained mercy of the Lord to be faithful <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">And he would have them look upon him as one that himself had received mercy from the Lord, and as he desired to be faithful in the discharge of his trust, so might and ought to have credit given him in what he said. In <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>uch sense we read in Scripture of a faithful saying, a faithful Crea<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>o<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> faithful man. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:443" />26 I suppose therefore that this is good <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Good here signifieth <ns0:hi>convenient</ns0:hi> (as before) if other cir<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cumstances of particular persons make it not sinful: or <ns0:hi>better</ns0:hi> with respect</ns0:note> for the present <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, <ns0:hi>necessity.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> distress <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">to the present distress or necessity, by which, without doubt, the Apostle meaneth, not the common necessi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ties of all men that are born <ns0:hi>once to dye,</ns0:hi> (which is the more easie the fewer relations we have to part from) nor yet of fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mily-troubles and concerns; for there is none who hath a family in this world to look after, but will have trouble in the flesh, but the continual troubles with which the Church of God was disquieted, as the Ark upon the waters, and the more special troubles of the Primitive Church; for though their great Per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />secutions from the Heathen were not possibly at that time be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gun, yet Christ had foretold them, and the Apostles had them in a very near prospect (<ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> is thought to have dyed the <ns0:hi>tenth</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>eleventh</ns0:hi> year of <ns0:hi>Nero.</ns0:hi>) For this present necessity or distress, the Apostle gives his opinion, That it was <ns0:hi>convenient</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>better</ns0:hi> for those that could honestly abstain from marriage, to keep themselves in their single and unmarried condition.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>I say,</ns0:hi> that <ns0:hi>it is</ns0:hi> good for a man so to be.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 Art thou bound unto a wife? seek not to be loosed. Art thou loosed from a wife? seek not a wife <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Art thou bound by marriage, or bound by contract, do not use any sinful ways to be loosed from that bond, either by divorce or by a voluntary departure: if the Unbeliever will depart, he or she may, you are not obliged to court their stay, but do not you put him or her away. Are you free from a wife, either as yet unmarried, or by the hand of God separa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted, in case you can without sin, abstain. If your circumstances be such, as they do not oblige you to marriage, do not seek a w<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>fe. The times are like to be full of trouble and difficulty. Our Master said, <ns0:hi>Wo to them that are with child, and give suck in those days,</ns0:hi> Matt. 24.19.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28 But and if thou marry, thou hast not sinned, and if a virgin marry, she hath not sinned: Never<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />theless, such shall have trouble in the flesh <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">I would not have you mistake me, as if I judged marriage sinful for persons in any state of condition, or of any Sex;</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">but those that are married in any time, will find troubles about the things of this life, and those that marry in such times as the<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> are, and you are like further to see, will meet with more than ordinary troubles of this nature, I only would spare you, and have you keep your selves as free as you can; or <ns0:hi>I spare you</ns0:hi> any further discourse of that nature, not willing to torment you before the time cometh.</ns0:note>: but I spare you.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="29">29 But <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. 13.11. 1 <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. 4.7. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. 3.8, 9.</ns0:note> this I say, brethren <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">He had before spoken to what concerned some, now he comes to what concerneth all.</ns0:note>, The time is short <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">The time (saith he) is <ns0:hi>short,</ns0:hi> furled up like sails, when the Mariner comes near his Port. He either meaneth the time of this life, or the time of the Worlds duration, we often find the Apostles speaking of their times as the last times (and in these senses all are concerned.) Or the time of the Churches rest and tranquillity, which they had hi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />therto enjoyed in a far more perfect degree, than they enjoyed them soon after this, when ten Persecutions followed imme<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />diately one upon the neck of another.</ns0:note>. It remaineth, that both they that have wives, be as though they had none <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Therefore (saith the Apostle) it is the concernment of all Christians, not to in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dulge themselves too much in the pleasures and contentments of this life; but if ye be married, or shall marry, you will be con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cerned to keep your hearts as loose from the contentment and satisfaction men use to take in their wives, as if you had no wives at all.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="30">30 And they that weep, as though they wept not <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">This consideration also should weigh with those who have a more afflicted portion in this life, and are mourners for the loss of their near relations, they have but lost what they could not long have kept, and for the time they kept them, must have enjoyed them probably with a great deal of sorrow and bitterness.</ns0:note>: and they that rejoyce, as though they re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />joyced not <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">And so for any of those who rejoyced in any worldly enjoyments, the shortness of the time they are like to have them to rejoyce in, should admonish them to govern and moderate their joy, for it is like to be but like the crackling of thorns under a pot.</ns0:note>: and they that buy, as though they possessed not <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">And those that have liberal possessions of good things in this life, they should look upon them as none of theirs, and use them as not like to be their possessions long.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="31">31 And they that use this world, as not abusing it <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">While you have any thing of this worlds goods you may use them, yea, you must use them, without them you cannot live in the world; but the consideration how little the time is you are like to have them to use, should govern you in the use of them, so as you ought to take heed you do not use them to any other purpose, or for any other end, than that for which God hath appointed and given them to you.</ns0:note>: For <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 39.6. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 2.17.</ns0:note> the fashion of this world passeth a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />way <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">For this world is like a Stage or Theatre where are diversities of <ns0:hi>Scenes,</ns0:hi> and the present <ns0:hi>Scene</ns0:hi> abideth but for a little time, then passeth, and another Scene or figure of things appeareth: those who ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pear this day in the form of Princes and Nobles, to morrow appear as beggers and persons of a low estate and degree.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="32">32 But I would have you without carefulness <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">The reason why I have advised (during the present di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stressed estate of the Church) a single rather than a married life, for those to whom God hath given the gift of continency, is, that those who are Christians might live as free from such cares as divide and distract men and womens minds, as they possibly can.</ns0:note>. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Tim. 5.5.</ns0:note> He that is unmarried, careth for the things that belong to the Lord, how he may please the Lord <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">The single person that hath a spiritual heart disposed to pious performances, being free from other distracti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons and cares, caused by worldly occasions, will spend all his thoughts about his duty toward God, and how to please him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="33">33 But he that is married, careth for the things that are of the world, how he may please <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> wife <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">But he that is married, hath other things which he must take care about; for besides that he is obliged to provide for his family, husbands and wives are under some obligations to please each other by divertisements, which though not in them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves sinful, yet take up time, which those free from such re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lations, may spend more religiously.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="34">34 There is a difference also between a wife and a virgin <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">There is the same difference betwixt a married woman and a single woman, as there is betwixt a married man and a single man.</ns0:note>: The unmarried woman careth for the things of the Lord, that she may be holy both in body and in spirit: but she that is married, careth for the things of the world, how she may please <ns0:hi>her</ns0:hi> husband <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">If a woman be unmarried, and be piously disposed, she hath leisure and opportunity enough to mind the things of God; but if she be married, she will then be obliged to attend secular affairs, to take care for her family, and to please her husband. It is the same thing that was before said of the man. The sense is, That a conjugal relation draws along with it many diversions, from which a single life is free.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="35">35 And this I speak for your own profit <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">For your advantage both as to your converse in the world, and also for your religious conversation, and the performance of those duties which you owe unto God; for those that are married, must meet with more troubles and cares in this life, and cannot have so much time and leisure for religious duties, as others have that are not intangled in the domestick cares of a family.</ns0:note>, not that I may cast a snare upon you <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Yet I would not bring you under a snare, imposing what God hath not imposed, and obliging you where God hath not obliged you.</ns0:note>, but for that which is comely <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">The word here is <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, it strictly <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ignifies a thing of a good figure, and is translated in Scripture <ns0:hi>honourable, Mark</ns0:hi> 15.43. <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 13.50. & 17.11. where it sig<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nifies what is of a fair and good repute in the eye of the world, which is also the sense of it, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 12.24. where we read of the <ns0:hi>comely parts</ns0:hi> of mans body; but in this place the word signifies most largely the same with <ns0:hi>profitable</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>convenient.</ns0:hi> For mar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />riage is a state which neither is in it self <ns0:hi>indecent,</ns0:hi> nor ever was so reputed in the World by any Nation, and the Scripture tells us, that <ns0:hi>Marriage is honourable amongst all.</ns0:hi> The word therefore here is of the same significancy with <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, which in the be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ginning of the verse is translated <ns0:hi>profitable,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 6.12. is translated <ns0:hi>expedient.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, and that you may attend upon the Lord without distraction <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">The phrase in the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> is very diffi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cult to be translated properly into our English language, word for word it is, <ns0:hi>To sit well to the Lord without distraction</ns0:hi>; our Translators render it, <ns0:hi>To serve the Lord.</ns0:hi> We have something like it in our language, when we express our diligent atten<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dance to a thing, under the notion of <ns0:hi>sitting close to a business,</ns0:hi> which is opposed to such an attendance to business, as we give when we have many avocations and callings away, so as we can<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />not sit close to it. The Apostle saith, That this was the end of his advising those who could contain not to marry under that state of things in the World referring to the Church, that they might with more ease and conveniency attend to the great con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cerns of their Souls, without those distracting and dividing thoughts, which they must have who were intangled with do<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mestick business and relations.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="36">36 But if any man think that he behaveth him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self uncomely <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">There is a general and a particular uncomeliness, some things are uncomely with respect to all persons, of such things the Apostle<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> doth not here speak; but of a particular uncomeli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness with respect to the circumstances of particular persons. Neither doth <ns0:hi>uncomely</ns0:hi> here signifie a meer indecency and un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />handsomness, but such a behaviour as suiteth not the general Rules of the Gospel, which judgment is to be ruled by the cir<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cumstances of persons, as they more or less desire marriage,</ns0:note> towards his virgin, if she passeth the flower of <ns0:hi>her</ns0:hi> age <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">if she be of marriageable years, or rather if she beginneth to grow old,</ns0:note>, and need so require <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">and be desirous of marriage, so as the parent seeth reason to fear, that if he gives not her in marriage, she will so despose of her self without asking her fathers advice or leave, and be exposed possibly to worse temptations: which two things seem to interpret that term, <ns0:hi>if need so require.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, let him do what he will, he sinneth not: let them marry <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">In such a case as this a Christian parent shall not sin, if he disposeth her in marriage, let her marry to such a person as she loveth, and her parent seeth proper for her. He speaks in the Plural num<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ber, because marriage is betwixt two persons. The reason of this determination is, because the Apostle in his former dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />course had no where condemned a married estate during the present distress of things, as sinful or unlawful, but only as inex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pedient, or not so expedient as a single life during the present distress, he had before determined, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 9. <ns0:hi>That it was better to marry than to burn.</ns0:hi> Now no inexpediency of a thing can ba<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lance what is plainly sinful. If therefore the case be such, that a man or woman must marry, or sin, though marriage brings with it more care and trouble, yet it is to be preferred before plain sinning.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="37">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:444" />37 Nevertheless, he that standeth stedfast in his heart <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">If a man be resolved to keep his daughter a Virgin, not uncertain in his own mind, and wavering what he should do, upon a just consideration of circumstances,</ns0:note>, having no necessity <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">and doth not see a necessity to dispose of her, either for the avo<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ding some sin against God, or for the better providing for himself and the rest of his family,</ns0:note>, but hath power over his own will <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">but hath a perfect freedom in his own will, so that his will be not contradicted by his daughters fondness of a married life; for in such a case the father, though he would willingly not dispose of his daughter in marriage, yet ought to be over-ruled by the will of his daughter, and so hath not a power over his own will, being forced by the rules of Religion to take care of the soul and spiritual welfare of his child; for though the parent hath a great power over his child, and ought to consent to the marriage of his child, yet he hath no such power, as wholly to hinder them from marriage.</ns0:note>, and hath so decreed in his heart that he will keep his virgin <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">If he be fully resolved upon a due consideration of all circumstances, and the Virgin be satisfied, and yields up her self in the case to her fathers pleasure,</ns0:note>, doth well <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">in such a case, if the father doth not put her upon marriage, but resolves to keep her unmarried, <ns0:hi>he doth well,</ns0:hi> that is, not only he shall not sin against God, but he doth that which is more eligible, considering the present cir<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cumstances of things, and better than if he did find out an hus<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />band for her, and give her to him (as it is expounded in the next verse)</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="38">38 So then, he that giveth <ns0:hi>her</ns0:hi> in marriage, doth well <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">There is no general rule for all parents in this case, where the duty or sin of parents may arise from their, or their chil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />drens different circumstances. But supposing that a parent ha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ving duly weighed all circumstances, be fully resolved, and he finds the childs will concurring, that she can forbear, and is willing to do in the case what her parent desires; in such a case as this, if the parent disposeth her in marriage, I cannot say he sinneth, but he doth what he may do.</ns0:note>: but he that giveth <ns0:hi>her</ns0:hi> not in marriage, doth better <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">But with reference to the present state of things in the Church and in the World, and with reference to the young womans liberty for the service of God, he doth better, if he doth not so dispose her. The thing is in it self indifferent, and Christians must be in it ruled, and inclined one way or another from circumstances.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="39">39 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 7.2.</ns0:note> The wife is bound by the law as long as her husband liveth: but if her husband be dead, she is at liberty to be married to whom she will <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">The Apostle all along this Chapter hath been speaking to several cases, which the Church of <ns0:hi>Corinth</ns0:hi> had put to him con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cerning marriage: some that concerned persons already marri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed: others that concerned such as were single, having been never married, he shutteth up his discourse with advice, which relateth to such as had lost their <ns0:hi>husbands,</ns0:hi> with reference to second marriages. As to this he determineth, That no woman might marry again while her first husband lived, that is, unless that her husbands be legally divorced from her for Adultery, or unless her husband, being an Heathen, had voluntarily deserted her: but if her husband were dead, she might marry to whom she would;</ns0:note>, only in the Lord <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">yet she was not at such liberty, as that she might marry an <ns0:hi>Vnbeliever.</ns0:hi> Unbelievers are either Heathens, or Christians in name; but such as are Idolaters, or profane persons, or Hereticks, who hold such Tenets as are inconsistent with any true Faith in Jesus Christ. This phrase, <ns0:hi>only in the Lord,</ns0:hi> seemeth to oblige godly women, not only to avoid mar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rying with Heathens, but with nominal Christians, that is, such who, although they have been baptized, and owne Christ with their tongues, yet hold such damnable Opinions, or live such profane lives, or worship God in such an idolatrous manner, as is inconsistent with any true Faith in Christ. The reason of the precept holds as well to the latter, as to the former.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="40">40 But she is happier if she so abide, after my judgment <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">But if other circumstances concur, that a widow can abide without marriage without waxing wanton, and running into temptation, and so as to manage her outward concerns without the help of an husband, my opinion is, That she is more <ns0:hi>happy,</ns0:hi> if she keeps her self a widow, and doth not marry again, not hap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />py, because more holy, or in a fairer road to the Kingdom of Heaven, but upon the two accounts before mentioned, more happy, because free from troubles and distractions, and be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause she will be more free and at liberty to mind heavenly things.</ns0:note>: And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Thess. 4.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
